2027-03-07.title: Fourth Sunday of Lent (Laetare)
readings: The wrath and the mercy of the Lord are shown in the exile and the release of his people
Let my tongue be silenced if I ever forget you!
Dead through our trespasses, by grace you have been saved
God sent his Son into the world so that the world might be saved through him
2027-03-07.alt: Year B. Laetare Sunday: rose vestments may be worn, and the organ and flowers, kept sober during Lent, may be used. Where there are catechumens, the Year A readings may be used every year, and they are always used at a Mass with the Second Scrutiny of the elect: 1 Samuel 16:1b, 6–7, 10–13a; Psalm 23:1–3a, 3b–4, 5, 6 (The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want); Ephesians 5:8–14; John 9:1–41 (the man born blind). The memorial of Sts Perpetua and Felicity is not kept this year because it falls on Sunday. No Gloria. Liturgical colour: violet or rose.
2027-03-07.verse: For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.
theo: The Fourth Sunday of Lent takes its old name from the first word of the Entrance Antiphon: Laetare, “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” We have passed the middle of the forty days, and the Church lets a little of Easter's light shine through. Where it is the custom, the priest wears rose instead of violet, as the sky lightens before dawn. The first reading tells the saddest chapter of Israel's history and turns it into hope. The leaders and people were “exceedingly unfaithful,” and they polluted the house of the LORD. Yet God “sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people.” They mocked the messengers and scoffed at the prophets, “until… there was no remedy.” Jerusalem was burned, the Temple destroyed, and the survivors carried off to Babylon. The Psalm gives voice to the exiles: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and there we wept when we remembered Zion.” Their captors asked for a song; they hung their harps on the willows. But the Chronicler does not end in tears. After seventy years, as Jeremiah had foretold, “the LORD stirred up the spirit of King Cyrus of Persia,” a pagan king, to send the people home and rebuild the house of God. The last word of the Hebrew Bible, in the order Jewish tradition keeps, is this invitation: “Let him go up.”

The Gospel is part of Jesus' night conversation with Nicodemus, a Pharisee and leader who came to him in the dark. Jesus recalls a strange story from the wilderness. When the people were bitten by poisonous serpents, God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, “and whenever a serpent bit someone, that person would look at the serpent of bronze and live.” “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.” In John's Gospel “lifted up” means two things at once: raised on the cross and exalted in glory. The very sign of our wound becomes the place of our healing. Then come the words many call the Gospel in miniature: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” God's first word to the world is not condemnation: “God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.” Judgment is what happens when the light comes and we choose: “people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.” Those who do what is true come to the light. Nicodemus himself, who came by night, will come into the open at the end, bringing a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial.

St Paul tells the same good news in other words: “But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.” We did not climb out of the grave of sin by ourselves: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” Grace comes first, always. But grace is not idle. Paul goes on: “we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.” Our fasting, prayer and almsgiving do not buy God's love; they are the fruit of a love already given. Where the Second Scrutiny is celebrated, the Church today reads the Year A Gospel of the man born blind (John 9), and prays that the elect may be freed from darkness and come to Christ, the light of the world. In both Gospels the movement is the same: from darkness to light, from the bite of the serpent to the healing of the cross, from exile to home. That is why we rejoice in the middle of Lent. The One lifted up draws all people to himself.
conn: Laetare.
The Entrance Antiphon begins with Isaiah 66:10: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” The same joyful pause comes in Advent on Gaudete Sunday. Rose vestments may be worn on both days.
Cyrus of Persia.
Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC and soon allowed exiled peoples to return home. Isaiah 45:1 even calls him the Lord's “anointed.” God works through rulers who do not know him.
Seventy years.
Jeremiah foretold seventy years of exile (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10). The Chronicler sees the land “keeping sabbath” while it lay empty.
The bronze serpent.
Numbers 21:4–9. Centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed it because people had begun to worship it (2 Kings 18:4). The sign was meant to point to God's healing, not to replace him.
Nicodemus.
A Pharisee and member of the council (John 3:1). He speaks up for Jesus in John 7:50–51 and comes openly with myrrh and aloes to bury him in John 19:39.
Lifted up.
Jesus speaks three times in John of being “lifted up” (3:14; 8:28; 12:32). It is the cross, and it is his glorification: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
altar: The Son lifted up on the cross is made present on the altar. At the elevation we look up at the Host and the Chalice, as the Israelites looked up at the serpent, and we live.
God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. In Holy Communion he still gives him to us, truly, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.
outline: Ask: what does it mean to rejoice in the middle of a time of penance?
Point 1 · By the rivers of Babylon
Sin leads to exile, but God's compassion has the last word.
Point 3 · God so loved the world
Not to condemn but to save.
Judgment is our choice before the light.
A rose vestment in the middle of violet: dawn before the day.
“For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.”
live: Look and live (John 3:14–15)
Spend five minutes this week gazing at a crucifix in silence, letting Jesus heal what has bitten you.
Learn John 3:16 by heart
Teach it to your children and pray it as a morning offering.
Come to the light (John 3:21)
Bring one hidden sin into the light of confession before Holy Week.
Rejoice
Do something joyful with your family today, as a foretaste of Easter, while keeping your Lenten resolutions.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

As those who looked at the bronze serpent did not perish from the serpents' bites, so those who look in faith at the death of Christ are healed from the bites of sin. Death came by the serpent; life comes by the death of Christ, which kills death.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
God did not give a servant, or an angel, or an archangel, but his only Son. Think how great is the love that gives what is most precious for those who are ungrateful.
St Gregory of Nazianzus (in substance)
We needed a God made flesh and put to death, that we might live. The serpent's poison was overcome by one lifted up on the wood.
magis: Catechism 458
The Word became flesh so that we might know God's love: “God so loved the world.”
Catechism 2130
The bronze serpent: images in the Old Covenant that pointed to salvation by the incarnate Word.
Catechism 679
Christ did not come to judge but to save; judgment is our acceptance or refusal of grace.
Catechism 1996–1999
Grace: the free and undeserved help God gives us, the source of our justification.
St John Paul II, Dives in Misericordia (1980)
The encyclical on God “rich in mercy” (Ephesians 2:4).
Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults
The Second Scrutiny, with the Gospel of the man born blind.
saints: St Casimir (4 Mar)

Prince of Poland and Lithuania (1458–1484), son of King Casimir IV, known for prayer, purity, love of the poor and devotion to Our Lady. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-five and is the patron of Lithuania.
Sts Perpetua and Felicity (7 Mar, not kept this year)

Two young mothers martyred at Carthage in 203: Perpetua, a noblewoman nursing her baby, and Felicity, a slave who gave birth in prison days before. Perpetua's own prison diary survives. They are named in the First Eucharistic Prayer.
This week
8 Mar: St John of God (commemoration). 9 Mar: St Frances of Rome (commemoration). 8–13 Mar: Lenten weekdays of the fourth week. 14 Mar: Fifth Sunday of Lent; Third Scrutiny.
2027-03-07.prayer: O God, who through your Word reconcile the human race to yourself in a wonderful way, grant, we pray, that with prompt devotion and eager faith the Christian people may hasten toward the solemn celebrations to come. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Father rich in mercy, you so loved the world that you gave your only Son. Draw us out of the darkness of sin into the light of Christ lifted up, give the elect the light of faith, and bring us rejoicing to Easter. Amen.

2027-03-14.title: Fifth Sunday of Lent
readings: I will make a new covenant, and remember their sin no more
Create a clean heart in me, O God
He learned obedience and became the source of eternal salvation
Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain
2027-03-14.alt: Year B. Where there are catechumens, the Year A readings may be used every year, and they are always used at a Mass with the Third Scrutiny of the elect: Ezekiel 37:12–14; Psalm 130 (With the Lord there is mercy and fullness of redemption); Romans 8:8–11; John 11:1–45 (the raising of Lazarus). From this Sunday, where the bishops' conference permits, crosses and images in the church may be veiled: crosses until the end of the Celebration of the Lord's Passion on Good Friday, images until the Easter Vigil. No Gloria. Liturgical colour: violet.
2027-03-14.verse: Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
theo: On the Fifth Sunday of Lent the Church stands at the door of the Passion. Two weeks remain before Easter, and the readings speak of an hour, a covenant and a seed. Jeremiah lived through the collapse of everything: the Temple destroyed, the king blinded, the people deported. The covenant of Sinai lay broken, “a covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, says the LORD.” Yet in that darkness God promised something no one had dared to imagine: “The days are surely coming, says the LORD, when I will make a new covenant.” It will not be written on stone tablets but within: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” No one will need to teach his neighbour, “Know the LORD,” “for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest… for I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more.” This is the only place in the Old Testament where the words “new covenant” appear, and Jesus will take them into his hands at the Last Supper: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.” The Psalm is the prayer of a heart that needs exactly this: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and put a new and right spirit within me.”

In the Gospel some Greeks, Gentiles who had come up to worship at the Passover, approach Philip with a simple request: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Philip tells Andrew, and the two of them, the apostles with Greek names, bring the request to Jesus. His answer seems at first to ignore them: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” All through John's Gospel the hour “had not yet come.” Now, when the nations begin to arrive, it has. And Jesus explains what glory means: “Very truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” The Greeks will see Jesus, and the whole world will see him, but only after the seed has been buried and has risen as a harvest. Then Jesus lets us see his heart: “Now my soul is troubled. And what should I say, ‘Father, save me from this hour’? No, it is for this reason that I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name.” This is John's Gethsemane. A voice from heaven answers: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” Some hear thunder; some think an angel has spoken. And Jesus says: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” He means the cross. The cross is not his defeat; it is the throne from which he draws the world.

The Letter to the Hebrews shows us the same hour from inside: “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.” He was heard, not by being spared death, but by being raised from it. “Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered,” and so became “the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him.” This is the law written on the heart: the Son's obedience, poured into us by the Holy Spirit. Jesus does not ask us to do what he has not done: “Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.” Every Christian life is a grain of wheat. We die a little in every act of self-giving, every forgiven injury, every Lenten sacrifice, and God turns it into fruit. Where there are catechumens, the Church today reads the Gospel of Lazarus and celebrates the Third Scrutiny, praying that the elect may be freed from the power of death. Both Gospels say the same: Jesus is “the resurrection and the life,” and the grave is the place where God's harvest begins. From today, in many churches, the crosses are veiled. It is a fast of the eyes, so that on Good Friday we may look on the Crucified with new hearts.
conn: The new covenant.

Jeremiah 31:31–34 is the only Old Testament passage that uses the words “new covenant”. Jesus takes them up at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes the whole passage.
Some Greeks.
Probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, sometimes called “God-fearers”. Philip and Andrew are the only apostles with Greek names; through them the nations come to Jesus.
The hour.
Again and again John says that Jesus' hour had not yet come (John 2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now he says: “The hour has come.” His hour is his Passion, death, resurrection and return to the Father.
John's Gethsemane.
John does not describe the agony in the garden; instead Jesus says here: “Now my soul is troubled.” Hebrews 5:7 describes the same struggle: prayers “with loud cries and tears.”
Lifted up.
In John the cross is an exaltation. Jesus is “lifted up” on the cross as the serpent was lifted up by Moses, and from there he draws all people (John 3:14; 8:28; 12:32).
The Third Scrutiny.
With the Gospel of Lazarus, the Church prays that the elect be freed from the power of sin and death and filled with the Spirit who gives life, before their Baptism at the Easter Vigil.
altar: Jesus said: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain. At the altar the Bread made from the grain becomes his Body, given for the life of the world. The seed that died is the bread that feeds us.
“This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.” At every Mass Jeremiah's promise is fulfilled: the covenant is renewed, and our sins are forgiven and remembered no more.
outline: Ask: what does a farmer lose when he plants a seed, and what does he gain?
Point 1 · A covenant written on the heart
Jeremiah's promise and the cup of the Last Supper.
Point 2 · Create in me a clean heart
The prayer of the repentant sinner.
Point 3 · We wish to see Jesus
The nations arrive and the hour comes.
A veiled cross and a buried seed, waiting for Easter morning.
“I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
live: Let God write on your heart (Jeremiah 31:33)
Choose one commandment you find hard, and ask the Spirit each day this week to write it on your heart.
Be a grain of wheat (John 12:24)
Choose one daily act of self-giving this week: a word held back, a service offered, an injury forgiven.
Help others see Jesus (John 12:21)
Bring someone to Mass, confession or the parish Way of the Cross before Holy Week.
Pray for the elect
Pray for those preparing for Baptism at the Third Scrutiny, that Christ may call them out of every tomb.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
Christ himself was the grain that had to die and be multiplied. He was sown in the earth in his Passion and rose again to bear the harvest of the Church throughout the world.
St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)
On his way to martyrdom in Rome he wrote that he was God's wheat, to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that he might become the pure bread of Christ.
St Leo the Great (in substance)

You drew all things to yourself, Lord, when you were lifted up on the cross. The cross is the source of every blessing and the cause of every grace, through which believers receive strength from weakness and life from death.
magis: Catechism 1965–1966
The New Law of the Gospel, written on hearts by the grace of the Holy Spirit, fulfils Jeremiah's promise.
Catechism 2606
Jesus' prayer “with loud cries and tears”: all the troubles of humanity gathered up in his offering to the Father.
Catechism 1431–1432
Interior conversion: God gives us a new heart (Psalm 51).
Catechism 662
“When I am lifted up from the earth”: the cross as the beginning of his exaltation.
Catechism 994
Jesus, the Resurrection and the Life: the raising of Lazarus as a sign of the resurrection to come.
Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults 171–177
The Third Scrutiny on the Fifth Sunday of Lent.
saints: St Frances of Rome (9 Mar)
Roman noblewoman (1384–1440), wife and mother, who nursed the sick through plague and war and founded the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi. She is a model of holiness in family life.
This week

15–20 Mar: Lenten weekdays of the fifth week (Preface of the Passion of the Lord). 17 Mar: St Patrick (commemoration). 18 Mar: St Cyril of Jerusalem (commemoration). 19 Mar (Friday): Solemnity of St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary; as a solemnity it is not a day of abstinence. 21 Mar: Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord.
2027-03-14.prayer: By your help, we beseech you, Lord our God, may we walk eagerly in that same charity with which, out of love for the world, your Son handed himself over to death. Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, grain of wheat buried for us, write your new covenant on our hearts. Create in us clean hearts, draw us to yourself from the cross, and call the elect out of every tomb into the life of Easter. Amen.

2027-03-21.title: Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord
readings: Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
I did not hide my face from insult and spitting; I know that I shall not be put to shame
My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
He humbled himself; therefore God also highly exalted him
The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Mark
2027-03-21.alt: Year B. Holy Week begins. The Lord's entrance into Jerusalem is commemorated in one of three forms given in the Roman Missal: the procession, the solemn entrance or the simple entrance. No Gloria; the Creed is said. The Passion is proclaimed without candles or incense, without the greeting and the signing of the book; all kneel for a short pause after the death of the Lord. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-03-21.verse: he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
theo: Palm Sunday has two faces, and the liturgy shows both. It begins with a joyful procession and ends in the silence of the tomb. Here is how the day unfolds, step by step, so that a family can follow it. 1. Gathering outside. Where possible, the people assemble outside the church, in another church, a hall or the parish grounds, holding branches; in Kerala these are usually tender coconut fronds, kuruthola, often woven into crosses and flowers. The priest and ministers wear red. 2. The opening acclamation. All sing “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel. Hosanna in the highest.” 3. Greeting and blessing. The priest greets the people, briefly invites them to accompany the Lord as he enters his city to accomplish his Passion and Resurrection, blesses the branches with a prayer and sprinkles them with holy water in silence. 4. The Gospel of the entrance. A deacon or the priest proclaims Mark 11:1–10 (or John 12:12–16): the two disciples, the colt never ridden, the cloaks and leafy branches, and the cry “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!” 5. The procession. After the invitation “let us go forth in peace,” the procession moves to the church: the thurible, the cross adorned with branches, candles, the Book of the Gospels, the clergy and then all the people with their palms, singing Psalm 24 and Psalm 47 and the ancient hymn “All glory, laud and honour to you, Redeemer King.” 6. Entering the church. As the procession enters, a responsory recalls the children of the Hebrews who went out to meet the Lord. The priest venerates the altar, goes to the chair and, omitting the usual introductory rites, says the Collect. Where a procession outside is not possible, the Missal provides a solemn entrance, with the blessing of branches near the church door or inside, or a simple entrance with the entrance antiphon.

Then the mood changes. The first reading is the third song of the Servant of the Lord: “I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting.” Yet the Servant is not crushed: “The Lord GOD helps me… therefore I have set my face like flint.” The Psalm is the one Jesus himself prayed on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” It describes with uncanny precision the mocking, the pierced hands and feet, the garments divided by lot, and then turns at the end into praise: “I will tell of your name to my brothers and sisters.” St Paul's hymn in Philippians gives the whole mystery in a few lines: Christ, “though he was in the form of God,” emptied himself, took the form of a slave, “humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him,” so that every knee should bend and every tongue confess “that Jesus Christ is Lord.” The procession of palms and the road to the cross are one movement: the King enters his city in order to give his life.

This year the Passion is read according to St Mark, the oldest and most stark of the four. It begins in Bethany, where an unnamed woman breaks an alabaster jar and pours costly nard on Jesus' head; he says she has anointed his body for burial and “what she has done will be told in remembrance of her.” At the Last Supper he takes bread, blesses, breaks and says, “Take; this is my body,” and over the cup, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.” In Gethsemane he prays, “Abba, Father, for you all things are possible; remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want,” while his friends sleep. He is betrayed with a kiss; “All of them deserted him and fled,” even a young man who runs away leaving his linen cloth behind. Before the high priest he is silent until asked whether he is the Messiah: then he answers plainly, “I am.” Peter denies him three times and weeps. Pilate, knowing Jesus is innocent, hands him over to satisfy the crowd; soldiers mock him with purple and thorns; Simon of Cyrene carries his cross. On the cross he is mocked by all, and at three in the afternoon he cries out the first words of Psalm 22. He breathes his last; the curtain of the Temple is torn in two; and a Roman centurion, a pagan, makes the confession that Mark's whole Gospel has been waiting for: “Truly this man was God's Son!” The women watch from a distance, and Joseph of Arimathea lays him in a tomb cut from the rock.

How the Passion is proclaimed. It is read without candles and incense, without the usual greeting, “The Lord be with you,” and without signing the book, because the Lord is going to his death. Often three readers share it: a narrator, a reader for the other voices, and the priest for the words of Christ, while the whole assembly speaks the words of the crowd. When we say “Crucify him!” we confess that it is our sins that crucified him; the Church teaches that the Passion cannot be blamed on all the Jews of that time or on the Jewish people today, and that all sinners were the authors of his suffering (Catechism 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). At the words “he breathed his last,” everyone kneels in silence for a moment. After a brief homily the Mass continues as usual. Take your blessed palm home and place it behind the crucifix or the family's holy pictures; next year it will be returned to be burned for the ashes of Ash Wednesday. Then keep this week holy: the Chrism Mass, when the bishop blesses the holy oils with his priests (often on Holy Thursday morning, in some dioceses earlier in the week); the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Thursday evening; Good Friday, a day of fasting and abstinence; and the great Easter Vigil on Saturday night. Because 25 March falls on Holy Thursday this year, the Solemnity of the Annunciation is transferred to Monday 5 April 2027, after the Octave of Easter.
conn: Hosanna.
A Hebrew cry meaning “save, we pray” (Psalm 118:25), which had become a shout of praise. The crowd adds Psalm 118:26: “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the LORD.”
The colt.
Zechariah 9:9 foretold a humble king riding on a colt, the foal of a donkey. A colt never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose (compare Numbers 19:2). Jesus comes as a king of peace, not of war.
Cloaks and branches.
Spreading cloaks was a sign of royal welcome (2 Kings 9:13). Leafy branches recall the feasts of Tabernacles and the rededication of the Temple (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7).
Three forms.

The Roman Missal gives three ways to commemorate the Lord's entrance: the procession from another place; the solemn entrance, with the blessing of branches at or inside the church; and the simple entrance, at Masses where neither is possible.
All glory, laud and honour.
The processional hymn Gloria, laus et honor was written by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, around the year 820.
Red vestments.
Red is the colour of the Passion and of the blood of martyrs; on Palm Sunday it also honours Christ the King entering his city.
The young man who fled.
Only Mark tells of the young man who ran off leaving his linen cloth (Mark 14:51–52). Many have seen in him a self-portrait of the evangelist, or an image of every disciple who flees.
The centurion's confession.

Mark's Gospel opens with “the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1); the first human being to proclaim him Son of God after his death is a Gentile soldier at the foot of the cross (15:39).
altar: The palms we wave and the Body we receive belong together. The King hailed with Hosanna gives himself on the altar as the one who said: “Take; this is my body.” At every Mass we sing the crowd's words in the Sanctus: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.”

The sacrifice of the cross that we hear today in the Passion is made present at every Mass, not repeated but offered once for all and given to us. Palm Sunday leads us straight to the altar of Holy Thursday and the cross of Good Friday.
outline: Hold up a palm frond and ask: how long does the joy of a welcome last?
The procession and the humble King on a colt.
Point 2 · The Servant who did not turn back
Isaiah 50 and Gethsemane: “not what I want.”
Psalm 22, the cross and the centurion.
A palm behind the crucifix at home, a reminder all year.
live: Take part in the procession
Come early with your family, carry your palm and sing; then keep it behind the crucifix at home.
Read the Passion again (Mark 14–15)
At home this week, read Mark's Passion slowly, one section each day.
Keep the Triduum
Plan now to be present on Thursday evening, Good Friday afternoon and at the Easter Vigil.
Watch one hour (Mark 14:37)
Spend an hour before the Blessed Sacrament this week, especially at the Altar of Repose on Thursday night.
fathers: St Andrew of Crete (in substance)

Let us run with him as he hastens to his Passion, and imitate those who went out to meet him. Not with garments or lifeless branches, but let us spread ourselves before his feet, clothed in his grace, so that we may receive the Word who comes.
St Leo the Great (in substance)
The cross of Christ is the source of every blessing and the cause of every grace. Through it believers receive strength from weakness, glory from shame and life from death.
St Augustine (in substance)

It was no great thing for the King of eternity to become King of men. He did not come to be king of Israel to demand taxes or to arm soldiers, but to rule minds, to lead believers into the kingdom of heaven.
magis: Catechism 559–560
The messianic entrance of Jesus into Jerusalem, celebrated each year on Palm Sunday.
Catechism 597–598
Responsibility for the death of Jesus: not the Jewish people as a whole, but all sinners are its authors.
Catechism 612–614
The agony in Gethsemane; Christ's death as the unique and definitive sacrifice.
Roman Missal, Palm Sunday
The three forms of commemorating the Lord's entrance and the proclamation of the Passion.
Paschale Solemnitatis 28–33 (1988)
Holy Week begins on Palm Sunday, which joins the royal triumph of Christ and the proclamation of his Passion.
saints: St Turibius of Mogrovejo (23 Mar, not observed this year)

Archbishop of Lima (1538–1606), he walked and rode thousands of kilometres to visit his vast diocese, learned the local languages, defended the indigenous peoples and founded the first seminary in the Americas. His memorial gives way to Holy Week.
This week

2027-03-21.prayer: Almighty ever-living God, who as an example of humility for the human race to follow caused our Saviour to take flesh and submit to the Cross, graciously grant that we may heed his lesson of patient suffering and so merit a share in his Resurrection. Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, King of humble peace, we greet you with palms and we follow you to the cross. 2027-03-25.title: Holy Thursday: Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper
readings: The law of the Passover meal: it is the passover of the LORD
Our blessing-cup is a communion with the Blood of Christ
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes
Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end
2027-03-25.alt: Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper. With this Mass Lent ends and the Sacred Paschal Triduum begins: one celebration in three days, from Thursday evening to Easter Sunday evening. The Gloria is sung and the bells are rung, then they fall silent until the Easter Vigil. Washing of feet; transfer of the Blessed Sacrament; adoration until midnight. Liturgical colour: white. CHRISM MASS: in the morning, or on another day close to Easter, the bishop celebrates with his priests the Mass in which the priests renew their promises and the oils of the sick, of catechumens and the holy chrism are blessed (Isaiah 61:1–3a, 6a, 8b–9; Psalm 89:20–21, 24 and 26; Revelation 1:5–8; Luke 4:16–21). ANNUNCIATION: the Solemnity of the Annunciation of the Lord, normally 25 March, falls today and is transferred in 2027 to Monday 5 April, after the Octave of Easter.
2027-03-25.verse: Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
theo: Tonight the Church enters the three most holy days of the year. Lent ends quietly before this evening Mass, and the Easter Triduum begins: the Lord's Supper, his Passion and death, his rest in the tomb and his Resurrection, celebrated as one great feast over three days. There is no final blessing tonight, and no greeting at the start of tomorrow's liturgy; the Church simply keeps vigil until the Easter Vigil ends with the Alleluia. Earlier today, or on another day this week, each bishop gathers his priests at the cathedral for the Chrism Mass. There the oils used all year for Baptism, Confirmation, the Anointing of the Sick and Holy Orders are blessed, and the priests renew the promises of their ordination. The Gospel of that Mass is Jesus in the synagogue of Nazareth: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me.” From the one Anointed, Christ, the anointing flows into the whole Church.

The first reading of the evening takes us back to Egypt, to the night of liberation. Each household is to take a lamb without blemish, slaughter it at twilight, put its blood on the doorposts and eat it in haste, “your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand.” “It is the passover of the LORD… when I see the blood, I will pass over you.” This night was to be “a day of remembrance… a perpetual ordinance.” The Jewish people have kept it faithfully to this day, and Jesus kept it with his disciples. Into this ancient memorial of freedom he poured a new meaning. He is the Lamb without blemish; his blood marks those who are saved; his Passover, from death to life and from this world to the Father, sets free not one nation from Pharaoh but every human being from sin and death. As St Paul says, “our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.”

Paul's account of the Last Supper is the oldest we have, written about twenty-five years after that night: “the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, ‘This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ In the same way he took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood.’” These words are not a parable. The Church believes, as she has always believed, that by the power of Christ's word and the Holy Spirit the bread and wine become his true Body and Blood, while their appearance remains (Catechism 1374–1376). The Mass is not a new sacrifice added to the cross; it makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary, so that “as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.” And with the command “Do this,” Jesus made the apostles priests of the New Covenant, so that this sacrifice would be offered “from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Malachi 1:11). Tonight we thank God for the gift of the Eucharist and for the gift of the priesthood.

St John does not tell the institution of the Eucharist. In its place he tells what it means. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” Jesus rises from the table, takes off his outer robe, ties a towel around himself, pours water into a basin and washes the feet of his disciples, the work of a slave. Peter protests: “You will never wash my feet.” Jesus answers: “Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.” The washing is a sign of the cross that is coming, where the Lord will be stripped and will pour out his life to cleanse us. And it is a command: “So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have set you an example.” The Eucharist and the towel belong together. Whoever receives the Body given for us must become bread broken for others.

Tonight's liturgy ends not with a dismissal but with a procession. The Blessed Sacrament is carried to a place of repose, and the people stay to watch with the Lord, remembering his words in Gethsemane: “could you not keep awake with me one hour?” (Matthew 26:40). The altar is stripped, and the church grows bare and silent. In 2027 Holy Thursday falls on 25 March, the day on which the Church usually celebrates the Annunciation, when the Word became flesh in the womb of Mary. The feast is moved this year to Monday 5 April. Yet the two mysteries meet: the body that Mary gave to the Son of God at Nazareth is the Body he gives us tonight in the Upper Room. Let us watch with him, and love as he has loved us.
conn: Step 1 · The Chrism Mass.

Celebrated by the bishop with his priests on Holy Thursday morning or another day near Easter. After the homily the priests renew their promises; later in the Mass (all together after the renewal of promises, or at the points the Missal gives in the Eucharistic Prayer and after Communion) the bishop blesses the oil of the sick and the oil of catechumens and consecrates the sacred chrism, breathing over it as a sign of the Holy Spirit. The oils are taken to every parish.
Step 2 · Lent ends, the Triduum begins.
Lent ends before the evening Mass. The tabernacle is empty at the start of the Mass; the hosts for tonight and for Good Friday will be consecrated at this Mass.
Step 3 · Gloria and bells.

The Gloria, silent all through Lent, is sung while the bells ring. Then the bells and the organ are silent (or used only to support singing) until the Gloria of the Easter Vigil. In many places wooden clappers are used instead.
Step 4 · The Word.

The Passover of Exodus, the Psalm of the cup of salvation, Paul's account of the Last Supper and John's washing of the feet. The homily speaks of the institution of the Eucharist and of the priesthood, and of the commandment of brotherly love.
Step 5 · The washing of feet (Mandatum).

After the homily the priest lays aside his chasuble, ties on a towel and washes and dries the feet of chosen members of the faithful, while the antiphons are sung. Since 2016 the Missal allows those chosen to be men and women, young and old, healthy and sick, clergy, consecrated persons and lay people, as a sign of the whole People of God. Then the Universal Prayer is said.
Step 6 · Gifts for the poor.
At the Preparation of the Gifts there may be a procession with gifts for the poor, while “Ubi caritas” (Where charity and love are, God is there) is sung.
Step 7 · The Eucharistic Prayer and Communion.
The Eucharistic Prayer has special words for tonight: “on the day before he was to suffer… that is today.” Enough hosts are consecrated for Communion on Good Friday.
Step 8 · The transfer of the Blessed Sacrament.

After the Prayer after Communion there is no blessing. The priest incenses the Blessed Sacrament and carries it under a humeral veil, with candles and incense, to the place of repose, while the hymn “Pange lingua” is sung. There it is placed in a tabernacle and incensed during the “Tantum ergo.”
Step 9 · Watching with the Lord.
The faithful are invited to stay in adoration. After midnight the adoration continues without solemnity. Some people visit the places of repose in several churches.
Step 10 · The stripping of the altar.
The altar is stripped of its cloths, and crosses are removed from the church or veiled. The people leave in silence. The Triduum continues tomorrow.
On the night when he was betrayed.
Paul (1 Corinthians 11:23) and the Eucharistic Prayer place the gift of the Eucharist on the night of betrayal: the Lord answers betrayal with the gift of himself.
The Annunciation transferred.
When 25 March falls in Holy Week or the Octave of Easter, the Annunciation is moved to the Monday after the Second Sunday of Easter: in 2027, Monday 5 April.
altar: Tonight the Lord says over the bread: this is my body that is for you. What lies on the altar after the consecration is no longer bread, but Christ himself, his Body given up and his Blood poured out, the one sacrifice of the cross made present.
Every priest stands at the altar because Jesus said tonight, do this in remembrance of me. Pray for your priests: without the priesthood there is no Eucharist, and without the Eucharist no Church.
The towel and the basin belong beside the altar. Whoever eats this bread is sent to wash feet.

fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

It is not man who makes the offerings become the Body and Blood of Christ, but Christ himself, who was crucified for us. The priest stands in his role and speaks the words, but the power and the grace are God's. This is my body, he says: this word transforms the things offered (cited in Catechism 1375).
St Ambrose (in substance)

Could not the word of Christ, which can make from nothing what did not exist, change things that exist into what they were not before? It is no less to give things their original nature than to change them (cited in Catechism 1375).
St Augustine (in substance)
Christians wash one another's feet whenever they forgive one another, carry one another's burdens and serve one another in humility. If we do not do it with our hands, let us do it with our hearts.
St Thomas Aquinas (in substance)
The Eucharist is the sacrament of love: it signifies love and produces love. In it Christ gives himself as food, so that what we receive we may become.
magis: Catechism 1337–1340
The institution of the Eucharist at the Last Supper and its meaning as the new Passover.
Catechism 1366–1367
The Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the cross.
Catechism 1374–1381
The Real Presence of Christ and the adoration of the Blessed Sacrament.
Catechism 611, 1337
At the Last Supper Christ made the apostles priests of the New Covenant.
Ecclesia de Eucharistia 1–5, 11–12 (St John Paul II, 2003)
The Church draws her life from the Eucharist; the Upper Room and Calvary.
Paschale Solemnitatis 44–57 (1988)
The celebration of Holy Thursday: the Chrism Mass and the Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper.
Decree In Missa in Cena Domini (2016)
The washing of feet may include all members of the People of God.

Normally kept on 25 March, nine months before Christmas. Because it falls on Holy Thursday this year, it is celebrated on Monday 5 April 2027, after the Octave of Easter.

2027-03-25.prayer: O God, who have called us to participate in this most sacred Supper, in which your Only Begotten Son, when about to hand himself over to death, entrusted to the Church a sacrifice new for all eternity, the banquet of his love, grant, we pray, that we may draw from so great a mystery, the fullness of charity and of life. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, on the night you were betrayed you gave us your Body and Blood, you gave us priests, and you washed our feet. Keep us with you in Gethsemane tonight, make us one at your table, and send us out to wash one another's feet. Amen.

2027-03-26.title: Friday of the Passion of the Lord (Good Friday)
readings: He was wounded for our transgressions
Father, into your hands I commend my spirit
He learned obedience and became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him
The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John
2027-03-26.alt: Good Friday. No Mass is celebrated today or tomorrow until the Easter Vigil. The Celebration of the Lord's Passion takes place in the afternoon, ideally about three o'clock: Liturgy of the Word with the Solemn Intercessions, Adoration of the Holy Cross, Holy Communion. The altar is completely bare, without cross, candles or cloths. Day of fasting and abstinence (abstinence from meat from age 14; fasting, one full meal, from 18 to 59; follow the norms of your diocese). The Collection for the Holy Land is taken up today. The Divine Mercy Novena begins today. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-03-26.verse: When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
theo: Today the Church does not celebrate Mass. The tabernacle stands open and empty, the altar is stripped bare, the bells are silent. On this one day of the year the Church gathers not to offer the sacrifice in sacramental form but to stand at the foot of the Cross where it was offered once for all. The first reading is the fourth Song of the Suffering Servant, written centuries before Christ: a man “despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering and acquainted with infirmity,” who goes silent “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.” And the prophet tells us why: “he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.” The Church has always read this song as the clearest picture of Good Friday in the whole Old Testament. The Psalm puts on our lips the words Jesus himself prayed on the cross in St Luke's Gospel: “Into your hand I commit my spirit.”

The Letter to the Hebrews shows us who is suffering. He is “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God,” and yet he is not distant from us: “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin.” In the days of his flesh he “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears,” and “although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.” That obedience, carried to the end, makes him “the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him.” So the reading ends with an invitation that fits this afternoon exactly: “Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness.” The Cross is that throne of grace.

Then we hear the Passion according to St John, read every Good Friday. John shows Jesus not as a victim dragged along but as the King who goes freely to his throne. In the garden across the Kidron he steps forward and asks: “Whom are you looking for?” When he answers “I am he,” the soldiers step back and fall to the ground. He heals the ear Peter has cut, and he goes with them. Before Annas he speaks openly; Peter, warming himself at the charcoal fire, denies him three times. Before Pilate he speaks of a kingdom “not from this world” and of the truth, and Pilate asks: “What is truth?” He is scourged, crowned with thorns, clothed in purple, and shown to the crowd: “Here is the man!” Carrying the cross by himself, he goes out to Golgotha. Over his head Pilate writes in Hebrew, Latin and Greek: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” The soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic. From the cross he gives his mother to the beloved disciple and the disciple to his mother. He says “I am thirsty,” receives the sour wine on a branch of hyssop, and says: “It is finished.” Then he bows his head and hands over his spirit. A soldier pierces his side, and at once blood and water flow out. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bind his body with spices and lay it in a new tomb in a garden.

Who is responsible for this death? The Church answers clearly. It is not “the Jews” of then, nor the Jewish people of today: the Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion “cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today” (Nostra Aetate 4). When St John writes “the Jews,” he usually means the Temple authorities of that time; Jesus, his mother and all the Apostles were Jews. The Catechism says that all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion, and that we Christians bear the heavier responsibility when we crucify him again by our sins (Catechism 597–598). So we do not point a finger today. We strike our breast. And we discover that the Cross is not first of all a crime but a gift: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). Love has gone to the end. “It is finished” is not a cry of defeat but the word of a work completed: the Father's will done, the Scriptures fulfilled, the world redeemed.
conn: How the liturgy unfolds (1): entrance in silence.

The priest and deacon, in red vestments, go to the bare altar in silence, without song. They prostrate themselves on the floor (or kneel), and everyone kneels and prays in silence. Then the priest says the opening prayer, without “Let us pray”.
(2) The Liturgy of the Word.

Isaiah 52–53, Psalm 31, Hebrews 4–5, then the Passion according to John, often read in parts by three readers. Candles and incense are not used for the Gospel. At the words “he gave up his spirit” all kneel and pause in silence. A short homily may follow.
(3) The Solemn Intercessions.

Ten great prayers for the whole world: for the Church, the Pope, all orders of the faithful, catechumens, the unity of Christians, the Jewish people, those who do not believe in Christ, those who do not believe in God, those in public office, and those in tribulation. For each, the deacon announces the intention, all pray in silence (they may kneel and rise), and the priest sings the prayer.
(4) The Adoration of the Cross.

The Cross is shown in one of two ways: either it is unveiled in three stages, or it is carried in procession from the church door with three stops. Each time the priest sings: “Behold the wood of the Cross, on which hung the salvation of the world,” and all answer: “Come, let us adore,” and kneel in silence. Then the people come forward one by one and venerate the Cross with a genuflection, a kiss or another sign of reverence, while the Reproaches (“My people, what have I done to you?”) and other hymns are sung.
(5) Holy Communion.

A cloth, corporal and the Missal are placed on the altar. The Blessed Sacrament, consecrated at yesterday's Mass of the Lord's Supper, is brought from the place of repose by the shortest way, with candles. All say the Our Father; the faithful receive Communion. There is no consecration today.
(6) Departure in silence.

After the prayer after Communion, the priest prays over the people with hands outstretched. There is no final blessing in the usual form and no dismissal: all leave in silence. The altar is stripped again; the Cross remains with candles for private veneration.
Why no Mass?

From the earliest centuries the Church has refrained from celebrating the Eucharist on Good Friday and Holy Saturday. The Sacrifice is present today not on the altar but on the Cross itself, which we contemplate and adore.
“The Jews” in John.

In John the term usually refers to the Temple authorities who opposed Jesus, not to the whole people. The Church forbids any use of the Passion to blame the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597).
Gabbatha and Golgotha.
Gabbatha (the Stone Pavement) was the place of judgement; Golgotha (the place of the skull) a rocky height outside the city wall, today within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
Hyssop and the Lamb.

A branch of hyssop was used to mark the doorposts with the blood of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:22). John notes that the legs of Jesus were not broken, as with the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46): he is the true Lamb.
altar: There is no Mass today, yet we receive Communion from the hosts consecrated at the Lord's Supper. The Body given on the cross and the Body given at the table are one and the same: the one Sacrifice of Christ.
Every Mass makes present this Sacrifice of Calvary in an unbloody manner. Good Friday teaches us what we receive at every altar: the Body that was given up and the Blood that was poured out for us.
outline: Point to the bare altar and the empty tabernacle, and ask: why is the church so empty today?

Point 2 · The King on the Cross

Blood and water from his side: the sacraments and the Church.

Approach the throne of grace with boldness.
People in a long line waiting to kiss a wooden cross.
“Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

Eat one simple meal, no meat; offer the hunger for those who suffer, and give what you save to the Holy Land collection or the poor.

fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Blood and water flowed from his side: water for Baptism and blood for the Eucharist. As Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, so the Church was formed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross.
St Augustine (in substance)
He hung on the cross, and the cross became a teacher's chair. From it he taught us how to love: he prayed for his persecutors and gave his mother into the care of his disciple.
St Andrew of Crete (in substance)

Had there been no cross, Christ would not have been crucified; had there been no crucifixion, life would not have been nailed to the tree; and death would not have been trampled underfoot. The cross is the trophy of our salvation.
magis: Catechism 595–598
The trial of Jesus; the Jewish people are not collectively responsible for his death; all sinners were the authors of his Passion.
Catechism 599–618
The redemptive death of Christ: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures”; the Lamb of God; the Cross as the unique sacrifice.
Nostra Aetate 4
The Second Vatican Council on the Church and the Jewish people.
Paschale Solemnitatis 58–72
The Congregation for Divine Worship (1988) on the celebration of Good Friday.
Code of Canon Law 1251
Good Friday, like Ash Wednesday, is a day of fasting and abstinence.

Begins today and continues until the Saturday before the Second Sunday of Easter (Divine Mercy Sunday, 4 April 2027).

2027-03-26.prayer: Remember your mercies, O Lord, and with your eternal protection sanctify your servants, for whom Christ your Son, by the shedding of his Blood, established the Paschal Mystery. Who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, King on the Cross, by your wounds we are healed. We adore you and we bless you, because by your holy Cross you have redeemed the world. Let the blood and water from your side wash us and feed us, keep us near your Mother at the foot of the Cross, and bring us with you to the joy of Easter. Amen.

The sacrifice of Abraham: God himself will provide the lamb
The Israelites walked on dry ground through the sea

2027-03-27.alt: Holy Saturday: the Church waits at the Lord's tomb, meditating on his Passion and death and his descent among the dead. No Mass is celebrated during the day, and Holy Communion may be given only as Viaticum. The altar remains bare. The paschal fast may be kept until the Vigil. The Easter Vigil, “the mother of all holy Vigils,” begins after nightfall and ends before daybreak on Sunday; it belongs to Easter Sunday. Of the seven Old Testament readings at least three are read (in serious circumstances at least two), and the reading from Exodus 14 is never omitted. Liturgical colour at the Vigil: white.
2027-03-27.verse: But he said to them, “Do not be alarmed; you are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look, there is the place they laid him.
theo: Holy Saturday is the day of the great silence. Christ lies in the tomb. The Church does not celebrate Mass; she keeps watch, like the women who rested on the sabbath according to the commandment and waited for the first light of the week. An ancient homily read in the Office of Readings today says (in substance): something strange is happening, a great silence reigns on earth, because the King is asleep; God has died in the flesh and gone to awaken those who have slept for ages. This is what we confess in the Creed: “he descended into hell.” Christ, truly dead, went down to the realm of the dead, not to suffer but to proclaim the good news to the just who had gone before him, Adam and Eve, Abraham, Moses, David, the prophets. Holy Saturday is the day of Mary's faith too: when all seemed lost, she kept believing. Many families keep this day quietly, preparing the house and the clothes for Easter, going to confession, decorating the church, and fasting until the Vigil.

When night falls, the Church begins the most important celebration of the whole year. It has four parts. First, the Service of Light. The church is in darkness. Outside, a fire is blessed. The priest prepares the paschal candle: he cuts a cross into it, the Greek letters Alpha and Omega, and the numbers of the year 2027, saying: “Christ yesterday and today, the Beginning and the End, the Alpha and the Omega; all time belongs to him, and all the ages; to him be glory and power through every age and for ever.” He may set five grains of incense in the cross, for the five holy wounds. The candle is lit from the new fire: “May the light of Christ rising in glory dispel the darkness of our hearts and minds.” The deacon carries it into the dark church, singing three times “The Light of Christ,” and all answer “Thanks be to God.” Little by little, everyone's candle is lit from it, until the whole church glows. Then the deacon sings the Exsultet, the Easter Proclamation: “This is the night” when Israel passed through the sea, when Christ broke the chains of death; it even dares to sing of “the truly necessary sin of Adam” and the “happy fault” that won so great a Redeemer.

Second, the Liturgy of the Word. Candles are put down, and the Church tells the whole story of salvation, as Jesus did for the disciples on the road to Emmaus: creation, Abraham and Isaac, the crossing of the Red Sea, God's everlasting love for his bride, the invitation to come to the waters, the wisdom of the commandments, and the promise of clean water and a new heart. Each reading is followed by a psalm and a prayer. Then the altar candles are lit, the Gloria is sung, and the bells, silent since Holy Thursday, ring out. St Paul tells us what has happened to us in Baptism: “we have been buried with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.” The priest intones the Alleluia three times, each time on a higher note, and the people repeat it: the Alleluia that fell silent on Ash Wednesday returns. The Gospel, from St Mark this year, tells of the women going to the tomb at sunrise with spices, wondering who would roll away the very large stone. They find it rolled back, and a young man dressed in white says: “Do not be alarmed; you are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here.” And then: “go, tell his disciples and Peter.” Peter, who denied him, is named: the first Easter message carries forgiveness.

Third, the Baptismal Liturgy. The Litany of the Saints is sung: the whole Church in heaven is called to stand with us. The priest blesses the baptismal water, often lowering the paschal candle into it, and the elect are baptized, and adults are confirmed at once. Then all the faithful, holding lit candles, renew their baptismal promises: we reject sin, Satan and all his works and empty show, and we profess faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The priest sprinkles everyone with the blessed water. Fourth, the Liturgy of the Eucharist. The newly baptized may bring the gifts to the altar and receive Holy Communion for the first time. For the first time since Holy Thursday the Holy Sacrifice is offered: the Lamb who was slain now lives, and gives us his risen Body and Blood. At the end the deacon sings the dismissal with the double Alleluia: “Go forth, the Mass is ended, alleluia, alleluia.” The long night of the world is over. Christ is risen.
conn: The paschal candle.

It stands for the risen Christ. It is lit at every Mass of the Easter season, then kept near the font and lit at Baptisms and funerals: the light we receive at the font is the light that leads us home.
Alpha and Omega.
The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet (Revelation 1:8; 22:13): Christ is the beginning and the end of all time, including this year, 2027.
The Exsultet.

An ancient hymn of praise sung by the deacon beside the candle. It praises even the bees that made the wax, and calls this night the night that “dispels wickedness, washes faults away, restores innocence to the fallen.”
Seven readings.
The full set runs from creation to the new heart promised by Ezekiel. Parishes may shorten it, but the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14) is always read, because Easter is the true Passover.
The return of the Alleluia.
Not sung since Ash Wednesday, it is solemnly intoned three times before the Gospel. Through the Easter season it is the Church's constant song.
“And Peter.”
Only Mark adds these words (Mark 16:7). The one who had denied the Lord three times is named personally in the first Easter message.
Descent among the dead.

“He descended into hell” (Apostles' Creed): Christ went down to the realm of the dead to free the just who had gone before him (1 Peter 3:19; 4:6; Catechism 631–637). Eastern icons show him lifting Adam and Eve by the wrist from their tombs.
Why at night?
The Vigil must begin after nightfall and end before dawn. Like Israel on Passover night, the Church keeps watch for the Lord who passes over and sets his people free (Exodus 12:42).
altar: At the Vigil the Eucharist is celebrated for the first time since the Lord's Supper. The newly baptized come to the altar for the first time; the whole Church eats the Passover of the risen Lamb.
Every Sunday is a little Easter. The Mass we celebrate each week is the same Paschal Mystery we keep tonight: Christ who died and is risen, truly present in his Body and Blood.
outline: Darkness, a single flame, and the cry: “The Light of Christ!”
Point 1 · The light that darkness cannot overcome
The new fire, the candle and the Exsultet.
Point 2 · The whole story of love
Seven readings: creation to the new heart.
Buried and raised with Christ in Baptism.
Go, tell his disciples and Peter.
A whole church glowing with candles lit from one flame.
“He has been raised; he is not here.”
live: Keep Holy Saturday quiet
Spend the day in prayer and preparation; keep the paschal fast until the Vigil if you can; go to confession if you have not yet.
Come to the Vigil
Bring the whole family to the Easter Vigil, even if it is long; children remember the fire, the candles and the bells.
Renew your baptismal promises from the heart
Before the Vigil, find the date of your Baptism and thank God for it.
Welcome the newly baptized
Greet and pray for those who are baptized or received into the Church tonight; offer to help them in their first year.
fathers: An ancient homily for Holy Saturday (in substance)

Something strange is happening: there is a great silence on earth today, because the King is asleep. He has gone to search for our first parent like a lost sheep. He takes Adam by the hand and says: Awake, O sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will give you light.
St Augustine (in substance)

This is the mother of all holy vigils, in which the whole world keeps watch. We keep vigil on this night because the Lord rose on it, and that life which knows neither sleep nor death began for us in his flesh.
Melito of Sardis (in substance)

He came from heaven to earth for the sake of the one who suffered; he clothed himself with that one in a virgin's womb. He is the Passover of our salvation, who rescued us from slavery to freedom, from darkness to light, from death to life.
magis: Catechism 631–637
Christ descended into hell; the meaning of Holy Saturday.
Catechism 1217–1222
Prefigurations of Baptism in the Old Testament, read at the Easter Vigil: creation, the flood, the crossing of the Red Sea.
Catechism 1168–1169
Easter, the “Feast of feasts,” and the Easter Triduum at the centre of the liturgical year.
Paschale Solemnitatis 73–96
Holy Saturday and the Easter Vigil: night, light, word, water and Eucharist.
Sacrosanctum Concilium 5–6
Christ redeemed us by the Paschal Mystery; the Church never fails to come together to celebrate it.
saints: The newly baptized
Tonight, all over the world, catechumens are baptized, confirmed and receive their first Holy Communion. Pray for them by name if you know them.
This week
28 Mar: Easter Sunday. 29 Mar–3 Apr: the Octave of Easter, each day a solemnity. 4 Apr: Second Sunday of Easter (Divine Mercy). 5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March).
2027-03-27.prayer: O God, who make this most sacred night radiant with the glory of the Lord's Resurrection, stir up in your Church a spirit of adoption, so that, renewed in body and mind, we may render you undivided service. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you lay in the tomb and went down among the dead to set them free. Keep us faithful in the silence, as your Mother was faithful. Tonight, light the fire of your love in our hearts, wash us again in the grace of our Baptism, and let us sing the Alleluia with our whole lives. Amen.

2027-03-28.title: Easter Sunday of the Resurrection of the Lord
readings: We ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead
This is the day the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad (or: Alleluia)
Seek the things that are above, where Christ is
Christians, to the Paschal Victim offer your thankful praises
He saw and believed: he must rise from the dead
2027-03-28.alt: Solemnity of solemnities. The Gospel of the Vigil (Mark 16:1–7) may be read instead; at an afternoon or evening Mass, Luke 24:13–35 (Emmaus) may be read. The Easter Sequence is sung (obligatory today). The renewal of baptismal promises with the sprinkling of water may replace the Creed. The double Alleluia is added to the dismissal throughout the Octave. The Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-03-28.verse: Then the other disciple, who reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
theo: “This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” Today the whole Church sings the Psalm of Easter. The stone the builders rejected, the man condemned and crucified on Friday, “has become the chief cornerstone. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes.” In the first reading Peter stands in the house of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, and tells the whole Gospel in a few lines: Jesus of Nazareth, anointed with the Holy Spirit and power, “went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.” They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, “but God raised him on the third day and allowed him to appear, not to all the people but to us who were chosen by God as witnesses, and who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.” The Resurrection is not a feeling or a beautiful idea. The Apostles ate and drank with the risen Lord; they touched him; they gave their lives for what they had seen. And Peter ends with an offer for everyone: “everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.”

St Paul tells us what the Resurrection changes in us. “So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.” Through Baptism our life is “hidden with Christ in God,” and when Christ who is our life is revealed, we too will be revealed with him in glory. Easter is not only something that happened to Jesus; it has happened to us. The alternative reading uses the image of the Passover bread: “Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch… For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed. Therefore, let us celebrate the festival… with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Then, before the Gospel, the ancient Sequence is sung: “Christians, to the Paschal Victim offer your thankful praises… Death and life have contended in that combat stupendous: the Prince of life, who died, reigns immortal.” And it turns to Mary Magdalene: “Speak, Mary, declaring what you saw, wayfaring,” and she answers: the tomb of Christ, who is living, the glory of Jesus' Resurrection, angelic witnesses, the shroud and the napkin.

The Gospel takes us to the garden early on the first day of the week, “while it was still dark.” Mary Magdalene sees the stone removed and runs to Simon Peter and the beloved disciple: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.” Two men run. The younger disciple outruns Peter, bends down and sees the linen wrappings lying there, but waits. Peter arrives and goes in. He sees the linen wrappings lying, and the cloth that had been on Jesus' head “not lying with the linen wrappings but rolled up in a place by itself.” No thief would unwrap a body and fold the cloth. Then the other disciple goes in, “and he saw and believed.” He sees signs, an empty tomb and folded cloths, and he believes in what he does not yet see: the living Lord. That is the way of faith for us too. John adds honestly: “as yet they did not understand the scripture, that he must rise from the dead.” Faith begins with a run, a look and a heart open to God; understanding grows afterwards.

The Resurrection of Jesus is the centre of our faith. He did not return to an ordinary life to die again, as Lazarus did. His true body, the body that was crucified and still bears the wounds, has passed into a new and glorious life that will never end. St Paul says plainly: “if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation has been in vain and your faith has been in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:14). But Christ has been raised, the first fruits of those who have died. Because he lives, sin does not have the last word, death does not have the last word, and the grave of everyone we love is not the end. This is why we gather every Sunday: every Sunday is the day of the Resurrection, a little Easter. And this is why we receive his Body: the risen Lord himself, truly present, gives us the seed of our own resurrection. At every Mass today the faithful renew their baptismal promises and are sprinkled with Easter water. Christ is risen! He is truly risen! Alleluia.
conn: Peter at Cornelius' house.
Acts 10 is the first proclamation of the Gospel to Gentiles: the Resurrection is good news for every nation, Jew and Gentile alike.
“Hanging him on a tree.”
An echo of Deuteronomy 21:22–23. The one who seemed cursed on the tree is the one God raised and made judge of the living and the dead.
The Easter Sequence.

Victimae paschali laudes, probably by Wipo of Burgundy (11th century). It is one of only four sequences kept in the Roman Missal (with Pentecost, Corpus Christi and Our Lady of Sorrows) and is obligatory on Easter Sunday.
The folded cloth.
The cloth (soudarion) that covered Jesus' head was “rolled up in a place by itself” (John 20:7). Grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body; the order in the tomb is a sign.
The beloved disciple.
Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle. He reaches the tomb first but lets Peter enter first: love runs ahead, and honours the one whom the Lord has placed first.
Renewal of baptismal promises.
At all Masses of Easter Sunday the Creed may be replaced by the renewal of baptismal promises, followed by the sprinkling of the people with water blessed at the Vigil.
Regina Caeli.
From Easter to Pentecost this Marian anthem (“Queen of Heaven, rejoice, alleluia”) replaces the Angelus at morning, noon and evening.
The Easter duty.
Catholics are bound to receive Holy Communion at least once a year, during the Easter season (Code of Canon Law 920), after confession if they are aware of grave sin.
altar: The Lamb who was slain lives. At the altar today we receive not the memory of a dead teacher but the living, risen Christ, truly present in his Body and Blood, the pledge of our own resurrection.
The Apostles were witnesses who “ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.” At every Mass the risen Lord still sits at table with his Church.
outline: Ask: if you had been there that morning, would you have run to the tomb?
Point 2 · Witnesses who ate and drank with him
The Resurrection is real and bodily.
Celebrate the feast with sincerity and truth.
A folded cloth in an empty tomb.
“This is the day the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad.”
live: Greet with the Easter greeting
Greet family and friends today and all this week: “Christ is risen!” and answer “He is truly risen!”
Keep Easter for fifty days
Keep the joy of Easter all season: pray the Regina Caeli, sing the Alleluia, and keep a festive meal on each Sunday until Pentecost.
Make your Easter duty
If you have not yet received Communion this season, prepare well and receive, after confession if needed.
Visit the lonely
Bring Easter joy and a share of your festive meal to someone sick, old or alone today.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (Paschal Homily, in substance)

Let no one fear death, for the death of the Saviour has set us free. He destroyed death by enduring it. Hell was embittered when it met him below. Christ is risen, and the demons have fallen; Christ is risen, and life reigns; Christ is risen, and not one dead remains in the tomb.
St Gregory Nazianzen (in substance)

Yesterday I was crucified with him; today I am glorified with him. Yesterday I died with him; today I am made alive with him. Yesterday I was buried with him; today I rise with him. Let us offer ourselves, the most precious possession to God.
St Augustine (in substance)

The Resurrection of Christ is the faith of Christians. That he died, even pagans believe; that he rose, only Christians believe. Let us sing Alleluia here, still on the road, so that we may sing it for ever in our homeland.
magis: Catechism 638–644
The Resurrection, a historical event attested by the empty tomb and the appearances to witnesses.
Catechism 645–647
The state of Christ's risen humanity: a true body, now glorious; the Resurrection as a transcendent event.
Catechism 651–655
The meaning and saving power of the Resurrection: it justifies us and is the principle of our own resurrection.
Sacrosanctum Concilium 102, 106
Easter, the greatest of feasts, and Sunday, the original feast day, the weekly Easter.
Code of Canon Law 920
The obligation to receive Holy Communion during the Easter season.
saints: St Mary Magdalene
The first witness of the Resurrection in John's Gospel; the Church calls her “apostle to the apostles.” Her day was raised to a feast in 2016 (22 July).
This week

29 Mar–3 Apr: the Octave of Easter, each day a solemnity, with the Gloria and the double Alleluia. 4 Apr: Second Sunday of Easter (Divine Mercy Sunday). 5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March).
2027-03-28.prayer: O God, who on this day, through your Only Begotten Son, have conquered death and unlocked for us the path to eternity, grant, we pray, that we who keep the solemnity of the Lord's Resurrection may, through the renewal brought by your Spirit, rise up in the light of life. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Risen Lord Jesus, you have conquered death and opened heaven. Let the joy of this day fill our homes. Raise us from every tomb of sin and sadness, teach us to seek the things that are above, and keep us faithful witnesses of your Resurrection until we see you face to face. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-03-01.title: Monday of the Third Week of Lent
readings: Go, wash in the Jordan seven times, and you shall be clean
My soul is thirsting for the living God: when shall I see him face to face?
No prophet is accepted in his own country. Many lepers in Israel, but only Naaman the Syrian was cleansed
2027-03-01.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. On any weekday of this third week, especially where there are catechumens, the Mass of the Samaritan woman may be used instead: Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 95; John 4:5–42.
2027-03-01.verse: Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in the prophet's hometown.
theo: Naaman is everything the world admires: commander of the army of Aram, “a great man and in high favor with his master,” a mighty warrior. But the reading adds one short sentence that changes everything: he “suffered from leprosy.” The way to healing begins with the smallest person in the story, a young girl from Israel taken captive in a raid, who serves Naaman's wife. She does not curse her masters; she wishes them well: “If only my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria!” Naaman sets out with letters, silver, gold and fine garments, expecting a cure worthy of his rank. Elisha does not even come to the door. He sends a messenger with a plain word: “Go, wash in the Jordan seven times.” Naaman is offended. He wanted a ceremony, a great man waving his hand over the spot. Are not the rivers of Damascus better than this muddy stream? Again it is the little ones who save him. His servants say: if he had asked something hard you would have done it; how much more when he only says, “Wash, and be clean.” Naaman goes down, immerses himself seven times, and his flesh becomes “like the flesh of a young boy.” And his heart is healed with his skin: “Now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.”

In the Gospel Jesus is in his own synagogue at Nazareth. The people who watched him grow up cannot accept that the carpenter's son speaks for God. Jesus reminds them of two old stories: Elijah was sent to a widow in Zarephath of Sidon, and Elisha cleansed “none of them… except Naaman the Syrian.” God's mercy has always gone out beyond the borders people draw for it, and it is often received by outsiders who know their need while insiders think they have no need. The townspeople are filled with rage and try to throw him from the cliff, “but he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.” The hour of his Passion has not yet come. In Lent the Church reads Naaman's story as a picture of Baptism: the proud man goes down into the water, comes up with the skin of a child, and confesses the one God. It is also a lesson for the baptized. God usually heals us through simple things: water, a word of absolution, bread and wine, a humble servant's advice. Pride wants something grand; grace asks only that we go down into the water.
outline: Ask: have you ever refused good advice because of who gave it?
Grace begins with the smallest person.
Point 2 · Go down into the Jordan
Pride wants something grand; God asks something simple.
Point 3 · No prophet in his hometown
“Now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.”
live: Go down into the water (2 Kings 5:14)
Bless yourself slowly with holy water today and renew your baptismal promises in your heart.
Listen to the little ones
Accept one piece of advice today from someone you usually overlook: a child, a servant, a younger colleague.
2027-03-01.prayer: Lord God, you healed Naaman the Syrian in the waters of the Jordan and opened his heart to know you, the one God. Heal us of pride, teach us to receive your grace in simple things, and let our thirst for you grow, until we come with joy to the waters of Easter. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Naaman wanted something grand and was healed by simple water. At the altar Christ comes to us in simple bread and wine, made truly his Body and Blood. The humble receive him with wonder.

2027-03-02.title: Tuesday of the Third Week of Lent
