readings: With a contrite heart and a humble spirit may we be accepted
Forgive your brother from your heart, not seven times but seventy-seven times
2027-03-02.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. On any weekday of this third week, especially where there are catechumens, the Mass of the Samaritan woman may be used instead: Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 95; John 4:5–42.
2027-03-02.verse: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, if another member of the church sins against me, how often should I forgive? As many as seven times?” Jesus said to him, “Not seven times, but, I tell you, seventy-seven times.”
theo: The first reading comes from the part of Daniel preserved in Greek, the prayer of Azariah in the fiery furnace. Three young Jews have refused to worship the golden statue of King Nebuchadnezzar and have been thrown into the flames. There, walking in the fire, Azariah does not complain or argue. He confesses: we have sinned; we have no ruler, no prophet, no leader, no burnt offering, no sacrifice, “no place to make an offering before you and to find mercy.” The Temple is gone. Everything Israel used to bring to God has been taken away. And so Azariah offers the only thing left: “Yet with a contrite heart and a humble spirit may we be accepted, as though it were with burnt offerings of rams and bulls… such may our sacrifice be in your sight today.” This is one of the great discoveries of the Old Testament, and one of the great lessons of Lent: when we have nothing else to give, God accepts a broken and humble heart. Azariah appeals not to his own goodness but to God's faithfulness, “for the sake of Abraham your beloved,” and to his “abundant mercy.” The Psalm makes the same plea: “Be mindful of your mercy, O LORD… Do not remember the sins of my youth.”

The Gospel shows what such mercy must do in us. Peter thinks he is being generous when he offers to forgive seven times. Jesus answers: “Not seven times, but… seventy-seven times,” that is, without counting. Then he tells the story of a servant who owed the king ten thousand talents, a debt so vast that a labourer could not repay it in many lifetimes. The king, “out of pity for him,” forgives it all. The same servant goes out, finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii, a few months' wages, seizes him by the throat and throws him into prison. The king's verdict is simple: “Should you not have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?” The parable is not about a God who loves to punish; it is about a heart that has received mercy and refuses to let it flow. We pray every day, “forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.” Lent asks us to make those words true. Forgiving from the heart does not mean pretending that a wrong was not wrong, or staying in danger; it means letting go of revenge and handing the debt over to God, as he has cancelled ours.
outline: Ask: is there a debt, of money or of hurt, that you are still holding someone to?
When we have nothing else to offer.
“Should you not have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?”
live: Offer a contrite heart (Daniel 3:39)
Tonight, before sleep, tell God honestly one sin you regret, and trust his mercy.
Cancel a debt
Forgive one person today from the heart; if it is safe and wise, tell them so, or at least pray a blessing on them.
2027-03-02.prayer: Lord God, merciful and faithful, you did not abandon the young men in the furnace, and you accept a contrite heart and a humble spirit. Remember your mercies, forget the sins of our youth, and teach us to forgive as we have been forgiven, not seven times but without counting. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Azariah had no altar and no sacrifice, only a humble heart. We have the one perfect sacrifice of Christ on our altars. Before we bring our gift, Jesus asks us to be reconciled with our brother or sister.

2027-03-03.title: Wednesday of the Third Week of Lent
readings: Observe the statutes diligently: this will show your wisdom to the peoples
I have come not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. Whoever does and teaches the commandments will be called great
2027-03-03.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. On any weekday of this third week, especially where there are catechumens, the Mass of the Samaritan woman may be used instead: Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 95; John 4:5–42.
2027-03-03.verse: Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
theo: Moses stands on the edge of the promised land and speaks to a people about to enter it. He does not hand them a burden; he hands them a treasure. “Give heed to the statutes and ordinances that I am teaching you… so that you may live.” The law of God is for life. And it is a sign to the nations: when other peoples see how Israel lives, they will say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and discerning people!” Then Moses names the real wonder: “For what other great nation has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is whenever we call to him?” The commandments are not the rules of a distant lord; they are the words of a God who has come near. That is why Moses ends with a warning and a duty: do not forget what your eyes have seen, and “make them known to your children and your children's children.” Faith is handed on in families, by memory and by example. The Psalm sings the same joy: God “declares his word to Jacob… He has not dealt thus with any other nation.”

In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says something that must have surprised his hearers: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.” Not one letter, “not one stroke of a letter,” will pass away until all is accomplished. Jesus does not throw away the law given through Moses; he brings it to its full meaning, from the outside to the inside, from the act to the heart, and above all he fulfils it in his own person, by his perfect obedience to the Father unto the cross. The Church has always taught that the moral law of the Ten Commandments still binds Christians, now lived in the freedom of the Spirit and the love of Christ. And Jesus adds a word for every parent, catechist and priest: “whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” Doing comes before teaching. In the middle of Lent this is a good day to ask: do I know God's commandments, do I keep them with love, and am I passing them on to the next generation by my life?
outline: Ask: what is one rule your parents gave you that you now understand was for your good?
The commandments as a treasure, not a burden.
Point 3 · Not to abolish but to fulfil
Jesus brings the law to its heart.
“Whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”
live: Make them known to your children (Deuteronomy 4:9)
Tonight, teach a child or grandchild one commandment and tell them why it makes life good.
Do before you teach
Keep perfectly one small commandment today that you usually take lightly, such as honest speech or Sunday rest.
2027-03-03.prayer: Lord our God, you are near to us whenever we call on you, and you have given us your law as a lamp for our path. Help us to keep your commandments with love, as Jesus fulfilled them, and to hand on the faith to our children by word and by example. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Jesus fulfilled the law by offering himself in perfect obedience to the Father. At every Mass that same obedient love is made present on the altar, and God comes nearer to us than Moses ever dreamed.

2027-03-04.title: Thursday of the Third Week of Lent
readings: This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the Lord their God
If today you hear his voice, harden not your hearts
If it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, the kingdom of God has come to you. Whoever is not with me is against me
2027-03-04.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. On any weekday of this third week, especially where there are catechumens, the Mass of the Samaritan woman may be used instead: Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 95; John 4:5–42. Commemoration of St Casimir (its collect may be used).
2027-03-04.verse: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come to you.
theo: Jeremiah's words today are among the saddest in the prophets. God reminds his people of the one thing he asked when he brought them out of Egypt: “Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.” But “they did not obey or incline their ear”; they followed “the stubbornness of their evil will” and “looked backward rather than forward.” Day after day God sent his prophets, and day after day they stiffened their necks. Then comes a hard sentence for Jeremiah himself: “You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.” And the final verdict: “truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips.” The Psalm turns this history into an invitation for today: “O that today you would listen to his voice! Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah.” The hardened heart is not one that has never heard; it is one that has heard many times and stopped listening.

In the Gospel Jesus heals a man who could not speak. The crowd is amazed; but some say he does it “by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons,” and others demand a sign from heaven. It is the same hardness Jeremiah lamented: they see the work of God and call it the work of the devil. Jesus answers with plain sense: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. Then the decisive word: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come to you.” The “finger of God” recalls Exodus, where Pharaoh's magicians admitted that the plagues were “the finger of God,” though Pharaoh's heart stayed hard. Jesus is the “one stronger” who overpowers the strong man and frees his captives. There is no neutral ground: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.” Today the Church remembers St Casimir (1458–1484), a prince of Poland and Lithuania who chose Christ over the glories of court: he prayed long hours, loved the poor, kept chastity, and was devoted to the Mother of God. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-five and is the patron of Lithuania. He listened to the voice of God in a palace full of other voices.
outline: Ask: is there a voice of God you have heard many times and stopped listening to?
Point 2 · Today, harden not your hearts
The danger of the deaf heart.
The stronger one who sets captives free.
“Whoever is not with me is against me.”
live: Listen today (Psalm 95:7)
Spend ten minutes in silence with today's Gospel and ask: what is the Lord saying to me?
Gather with Christ
Do one thing today that builds up the parish or family rather than scattering it: a word of peace, help with a task, an invitation to prayer.
2027-03-04.prayer: Lord God, you have spoken to us again and again through your prophets and in your Son. Soften our hearts so that today we may hear your voice; free us from every power of evil by the finger of your Spirit; and through the prayers of St Casimir keep us faithful to you amid the noise of the world. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The stronger one who overpowers the strong man gives himself to us at the altar. Each Holy Communion is a victory of Christ over the evil one in us, if we open our hearts to him.

2027-03-05.title: Friday of the Third Week of Lent
readings: Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God. I will heal their disloyalty; I will love them freely
I am the Lord your God: hear my voice
The Lord our God is the one Lord, and you shall love him
2027-03-05.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. On any weekday of this third week, especially where there are catechumens, the Mass of the Samaritan woman may be used instead: Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 95; John 4:5–42. Friday of Lent: abstinence from meat (or another penance as your bishops' conference determines). Many parishes pray the Way of the Cross today. Today is also the first Friday of March, when many keep the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.
2027-03-05.verse: Jesus answered, “The first is, ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.’
theo: The book of Hosea ends with one of the most beautiful invitations in the Bible. The prophet has spent fourteen chapters naming Israel's unfaithfulness, using the painful image of a wife who leaves her husband for other lovers. Now God himself teaches his people the words of their return: “Take words with you and return to the LORD; say to him, ‘Take away all guilt; accept that which is good.’” They are to renounce the false securities they trusted: “Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses; we will say no more, ‘Our God,’ to the work of our hands.” And then God answers with pure tenderness: “I will heal their disloyalty; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them. I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily, he shall strike root like the forests of Lebanon.” This is what conversion looks like from God's side: not a grudging acceptance, but a garden in bloom. The Psalm echoes the same longing: “O that my people would listen to me… I would feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you.”

In the Gospel a scribe asks Jesus the question every teacher of the law discussed: “Which commandment is the first of all?” Jesus answers with the Shema, the prayer devout Jews still pray every morning and evening: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.” Then, without being asked, he adds a second: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” The two cannot be separated. The scribe agrees warmly: this “is much more important than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” Jesus looks at him and says: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” Not far, but not yet inside. What is still missing? Jesus himself: the one who loves the Father with his whole being and loves his neighbour to the point of laying down his life. On this Lenten Friday, at the foot of the Cross, we see the two great commandments joined in one act of love. Return to the Lord, says Hosea; love him with all your heart, says Jesus. Both lead to the same place: the pierced Heart of Christ, from which healing and new life flow like dew.
outline: Ask: if someone measured your love for God by your calendar and your wallet, what would they conclude?
God teaches us how to return.
God's free love makes us blossom.
All your heart, soul, mind and strength.
Point 4 · Not far from the kingdom
The love that is still missing.
“I will heal their disloyalty; I will love them freely.”
live: Take words with you (Hosea 14:2)
Write a short prayer of return in your own words and pray it before the crucifix today.
Love with all your strength (Mark 12:30)
Give one hour of your strength today to someone in need: an errand, a visit, help with work.
2027-03-05.prayer: Lord our God, you are the one Lord, and you call us to return to you with words of sorrow and hearts full of love. Heal our unfaithfulness, love us freely, be like the dew upon us, and teach us to love you with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves, after the example of your Son's pierced Heart. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The scribe said that love is more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices. On the altar Christ offers the one sacrifice that is pure love: his Body given and his Blood poured out, the love of God and neighbour made one.

2027-03-06.title: Saturday of the Third Week of Lent
readings: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings
It is mercy I desire, and not sacrifice
The tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee
2027-03-06.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. On any weekday of this third week, especially where there are catechumens, the Mass of the Samaritan woman may be used instead: Exodus 17:1–7; Psalm 95; John 4:5–42.
2027-03-06.verse: But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even look up to heaven, but was beating his breast and saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
theo: The first reading opens with a beautiful song of repentance: “Come, let us return to the LORD; for it is he who has torn, and he will heal us… After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up.” The Fathers of the Church heard in these words a hidden promise of the Resurrection on the third day. But God's reply is sobering: “What shall I do with you, O Ephraim?… Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes away early.” The people's repentance is sincere for an hour and then evaporates in the sun. God wants something deeper and more lasting: “For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.” The Hebrew word for steadfast love, hesed, means faithful, covenant love, the kind that does not dry up by noon. Jesus himself quoted this verse twice when he was criticized for eating with sinners: “Go and learn what this means, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’” The Psalm, David's great prayer of repentance, gives us the words: “The sacrifice acceptable to God is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.”

In the Gospel two men go up to the Temple to pray. The Pharisee stands by himself and gives thanks, but only for himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like other people: thieves, rogues, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of all my income.” Everything he says is true. He really fasts and really gives. But he has come to God to be admired, and he looks down on his neighbour. The tax collector, a man despised as a collaborator with Rome, stands far off, will not lift his eyes, beats his breast, and says only: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Jesus says this man “went down to his home justified rather than the other.” The parable is told, Luke says, “to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded others with contempt.” It is a warning to every devout person, especially in Lent, when our fasting and almsgiving can quietly become a mirror. The tax collector's prayer has become one of the treasures of the Church: the Jesus Prayer of the East, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner,” grew from it, and at every Mass we strike our breast with him at the Confiteor. On this Saturday before Laetare Sunday, it is a good day to go to confession and to pray his prayer.
outline: Ask: when you pray, do you compare yourself with others?
Point 1 · Love like a morning cloud
Point 3 · Two men went up to pray
Point 4 · God, be merciful to me
“All who humble themselves will be exalted.”
live: Pray the tax collector's prayer (Luke 18:13)
Repeat slowly today, with your breathing: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.
Stop comparing
Each time you catch yourself judging someone today, say a blessing for them instead.
2027-03-06.prayer: Merciful God, you desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, and you do not despise a broken and contrite heart. Free us from pride and from contempt for others; make our love faithful and not like the morning dew; and let us go down to our homes justified, praying with the tax collector: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Before we approach the altar we strike our breast and say: through my fault. At the Lamb of God we confess: Lord, I am not worthy. Like the tax collector, we come to the Eucharist as sinners who trust in mercy, and we go home justified.

2027-03-08.title: Monday of the Fourth Week of Lent
readings: I am about to create new heavens and a new earth
I will praise you, Lord, for you have rescued me
2027-03-08.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. Commemoration of St John of God, religious (his collect may be used). On any weekday of this week the optional Mass of the Fourth Week of Lent may be used instead, with the Gospel of the man born blind (Micah 7:7–9; Psalm 27; John 9:1–41), especially where it was not read on Sunday.
2027-03-08.verse: Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and started on his way.
theo: Laetare Sunday has just lifted our eyes toward Easter, and today Isaiah carries that joy further. God speaks like an artist about to begin his greatest work: “For I am about to create new heavens and a new earth; the former things shall not be remembered or come to mind.” Jerusalem will be a joy and its people a delight; “no more shall the sound of weeping be heard in it, or the cry of distress.” No infant will die after a few days, and the old will live out their years; people will build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit. It is the picture of a world healed of death and of wasted labour. The Psalm answers with the song of someone who has been brought back from the edge of the grave: “O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me.” And it gives Lent one of its loveliest lines: “Weeping may linger for the night, but joy comes with the morning.”

The Gospel shows the new creation beginning in one household. Jesus has come back to Cana, where he changed water into wine. A royal official, probably a servant of Herod Antipas, walks some twenty-five kilometres up from Capernaum, because his son is dying. Jesus seems to answer coldly: “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.” The father does not argue; he simply pleads: “Sir, come down before my little boy dies.” Then Jesus gives him not a sign but a word: “Go; your son will live.” And the man does the hardest thing a worried father can do: he turns round and walks home with nothing in his hands but that word. “The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and started on his way.” On the road his servants meet him: the boy is alive, and the fever left him at one in the afternoon, the very hour Jesus spoke. Faith that began as a cry becomes trust in a word, and ends as the faith of a whole household. Today we also remember St John of God (1495–1550), a Portuguese soldier and bookseller who, converted by a sermon of St John of Avila, spent the rest of his life gathering the sick and the poor of Granada into a hospital and caring for them with his own hands. From his companions grew the Brothers Hospitallers. He believed that every sick person was Christ, and he served them like a father carrying home a child.
outline: Ask: have you ever had to walk away from a problem with only a promise in your hands?
Isaiah's new heavens and new earth.
Point 2 · Go; your son will live
A father who believes the word.
St John of God and the healing of Christ.
“Weeping may linger for the night, but joy comes with the morning.”
live: Believe the word (John 4:50)
Take one promise of God from today's readings and carry it with you all day, like the father walking home.
Visit the sick
Like St John of God, visit or call someone who is ill, and pray with them if they wish.
2027-03-08.prayer: Lord God, you make all things new and turn our mourning into dancing. Give us the faith of the royal official, to believe your Son's word and set out on our way. Through the prayers of St John of God, give the sick tender care and make our hands ready to serve them. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The word that healed the official's son from far away is the same word that is spoken over the bread and wine at Mass. We believe it, and Christ is truly present, giving life.

2027-03-09.title: Tuesday of the Fourth Week of Lent
readings: I saw water flowing from the temple, and all who were touched by it were saved
The Lord of hosts is with us; our stronghold is the God of Jacob
At once the man was made well
2027-03-09.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. Commemoration of St Frances of Rome, religious (her collect may be used).
2027-03-09.verse: When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be made well?”
theo: Today's readings are full of water. In Ezekiel's vision an angel leads the prophet to the door of the Temple, and from under the threshold a stream is flowing east. The angel measures a thousand cubits and the water is ankle-deep; another thousand and it is knee-deep; then up to the waist; then “a river that could not be crossed.” This river flows down into the Dead Sea, the lowest and saltiest water on earth, where nothing lives, and makes it fresh: “everything will live where the river goes.” On its banks grow trees whose fruit never fails and whose “leaves are for healing,” “because the water for them flows from the sanctuary.” Lent is leading the elect toward the waters of Baptism, and leading all of us to renew our own. The Psalm sings of the same river: “There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God,” for “the LORD of hosts is with us.”

The Gospel takes us to a pool in Jerusalem, Beth-zatha, with five porticoes full of the blind, the lame and the paralysed. Archaeologists have uncovered its great basins near the Sheep Gate. One man has been ill for thirty-eight years, almost a lifetime. Jesus sees him, knows how long he has lain there, and asks a surprising question: “Do you want to be made well?” The man's answer is the saddest sentence in the passage: “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool.” Then Jesus does what the water never did for him: “Stand up, take your mat and walk.” At once he is healed. Because it is the sabbath, the authorities object; John, writing after the break between Church and synagogue, often uses “the Jews” for these Temple leaders who opposed Jesus, not for the Jewish people as a whole, whom the Church honours as the people of the covenant. Later Jesus finds the man in the Temple: “See, you have been made well! Do not sin any more.” The healing of the body points to the deeper healing of the soul. The true river from the Temple is Christ himself, and his water reaches us in Baptism and in Confession. Today we also remember St Frances of Rome (1384–1440), a noblewoman married at thirteen, mother of three, who nursed the sick through plague and war, opened her house to the poor, and founded a community of Oblates. She used to say (in substance) that a wife and mother must sometimes leave God at the altar to find him in her housework. For many, she was the someone who carried them to the water.
outline: Ask: is there anyone in your life who could say, “I have no one”?
Point 1 · The river from the Temple
Ezekiel's water that makes the dead sea live.
Point 2 · Do you want to be made well?
St Frances of Rome and the people with no one.
“Everything will live where the river goes.”
live: Renew your Baptism (Ezekiel 47:9)
Bless yourself slowly with holy water today, remembering the river that first touched you.
Be someone's someone (John 5:7)
Find one person who has no one to help them, and help them this week.
2027-03-09.prayer: Lord God, from your sanctuary flows a river that brings life wherever it goes. Let the waters of Baptism heal what is sick in us, and give us the courage to answer Jesus when he asks if we want to be made well. Through the prayers of St Frances of Rome, make our homes places of prayer and service. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: From the pierced side of Christ on the cross flowed blood and water, the river of the sacraments. At the altar we drink from that river, and it makes us live.

2027-03-10.title: Wednesday of the Fourth Week of Lent
readings: I have given you as a covenant to the people. Can a woman forget her nursing child? I will not forget you
The Lord is gracious and merciful
As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whomever he wishes
2027-03-10.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet.
2027-03-10.verse: Can a woman forget her nursing child, or show no compassion for the child of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.
theo: The exiles in Babylon had a heavy thought: God has left us. “Zion said, ‘The LORD has forsaken me, my Lord has forgotten me.’” Isaiah answers with a promise of homecoming: in “a time of favor” God will say to the prisoners, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves.” He will lead them like a shepherd by springs of water; he will turn mountains into roads; heaven and earth will sing. Then comes one of the tenderest lines in all Scripture. God compares himself to a mother: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, or show no compassion for the child of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.” The Hebrew word for compassion is close to the word for womb; God's mercy is a mother's love from deep within. And the next verse, which the Lectionary leaves just outside today's reading, says: “See, I have inscribed you on the palms of my hands.” The Psalm sums it up: “The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.”

In the Gospel Jesus answers those who were angry that he healed on the sabbath: “My Father is still working, and I also am working.” God rested on the seventh day of creation, but he never stops giving life and judging the world; and Jesus does the same work as the Father. His hearers understand at once that he is “making himself equal to God.” Jesus does not take back the claim; he explains it. The Son does nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing; the Father loves the Son and shows him everything. “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.” Here Lent opens a window onto Easter. “Anyone who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life… and has passed from death to life.” And one day “all who are in their graves will hear his voice and will come out.” The God who cannot forget his children has sent his Son, who will not leave them in the grave. That is why we can face our own fears of being forgotten, of failure and of death, with hope.
outline: Ask: have you ever felt forgotten by God?
Point 1 · I will not forget you
Point 2 · My Father is still working
The Son does the works of the Father.
The voice that will call us from the grave.
“See, I have inscribed you on the palms of my hands.”
live: Remember you are remembered (Isaiah 49:15)
Write your name on a small card, with the words of Isaiah 49:16, and keep it in your Bible.
Pass from death to life (John 5:24)
Spend ten minutes today listening to the Gospel of the day, slowly, as Jesus' word to you.
2027-03-10.prayer: Father of mercy, you love us more than a mother loves her child, and you have written our names on the palms of your hands. When we feel forgotten, let us hear the voice of your Son, who gives life to the dead. Bring us with the elect from death to life this Easter. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: In the Eucharist the Son who gives life to whomever he wishes gives us his own life. Those hands which bear the marks of the nails still hold us, and do not forget us.

2027-03-11.title: Thursday of the Fourth Week of Lent
readings: Turn from your fierce wrath; change your mind and do not bring disaster on your people
Remember us, O Lord, as you favor your people
Your accuser is Moses, on whom you have set your hope
2027-03-11.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet.
2027-03-11.verse: You search the scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that testify on my behalf. Yet you refuse to come to me to have life.
theo: At the foot of Sinai, only weeks after the covenant, the people grow tired of waiting for Moses and make a calf of gold. God says to Moses: “Go down at once! Your people… have acted perversely.” They have “cast for themselves an image of a calf” and said, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” The Psalm puts it sharply: “They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass.” Then God tests Moses: “Now let me alone, so that my wrath may burn hot against them… and of you I will make a great nation.” Moses refuses the offer. He stands, as the Psalm says, “in the breach,” between God and the people, and pleads: they are your people, whom you brought out of Egypt; what will the nations say? “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants.” And “the LORD changed his mind about the disaster that he planned to bring on his people.” God does not change like a moody human being; Scripture speaks in human terms to show that he has willed to let the prayer of his friends shape history. Moses is the great intercessor, and a figure of Christ, who “always lives to make intercession” for us.

In the Gospel Jesus calls witnesses, as in a court. John the Baptist testified: he was “a burning and shining lamp.” The works the Father gave Jesus to do testify. The Father himself testifies. And the Scriptures testify: “You search the scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that testify on my behalf. Yet you refuse to come to me to have life.” It is possible to know the Bible well and still miss the Person to whom it points. Then a surprise: “Your accuser is Moses, on whom you have set your hope… he wrote about me.” The same Moses who once pleaded for a sinful people now bears witness to Jesus. Jesus is speaking to the religious leaders who opposed him, not condemning the Jewish people; the Church received from Israel the Scriptures, the covenants and the promises, and reads Moses with deep reverence. The question is for us too: do we read the Scriptures in order to come to Christ? Lent invites us to put away our own golden calves, the things we worship instead of God, and to come to the One of whom the whole of Scripture speaks.
outline: Ask: what do people today put in God's place?
Exchanging God's glory for an idol.
Reading the Bible to come to Christ.
“Remember us, O Lord, as you favor your people.”
live: Name your golden calf (Exodus 32:8)
Ask honestly: what do I trust more than God? Give it back to him today.
Stand in the breach
Pray today, by name, for someone who has turned away from God.
2027-03-11.prayer: Lord God, you listened to the prayer of Moses and spared your people. Free us from every golden calf, and give us hearts that intercede for others. Open our minds to understand the Scriptures, that we may come to your Son and have life. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Christ our High Priest, the true Moses, stands between God and us and offers himself for sinners. At every Mass his sacrifice is made present, and his intercession is our hope.

2027-03-12.title: Friday of the Fourth Week of Lent
readings: Let us condemn him to a shameful death
The Lord is close to the brokenhearted
They tried to arrest him, but his hour had not yet come
2027-03-12.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. Friday of Lent: abstinence from meat (or another penance as your bishops' conference determines). Many parishes pray the Way of the Cross today.
2027-03-12.verse: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit.
theo: As Lent moves toward the Passion, the readings begin to sound like the plotting of Holy Week. The Book of Wisdom, written in Greek by a Jewish teacher in Alexandria not long before Christ, lets us overhear the thoughts of the ungodly. They have decided that life is short and ends in nothing, so they will enjoy it and crush anyone who gets in the way. And the one who gets in the way is the righteous man: “Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is inconvenient to us and opposes our actions.” His very life is a rebuke to them: “the very sight of him is a burden to us, because his manner of life is unlike that of others.” He calls God his Father. So they decide to test him: “if the righteous man is God's child, he will help him.” “Let us test him with insult and torture… Let us condemn him to a shameful death.” Christians have always heard in these words the voices at the foot of the cross: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43). But the Wisdom writer adds the decisive line: “they did not know the secret purposes of God.” The Psalm gives the answer of faith: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit… He keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken”, words that John will see fulfilled on Calvary (John 19:36).

In the Gospel the danger is real. Jesus stays in Galilee because in Judea some were looking for a chance to kill him; when he goes up for the feast of Booths, he goes “not publicly but as it were in secret.” In John's Gospel “the Jews” here means the Jerusalem authorities who opposed Jesus; Jesus, his mother, his disciples and the crowds who welcomed him were themselves Jews, and the Church firmly rejects any blame of the Jewish people for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597). In the Temple, people argue: is this the Messiah? “Yet we know where this man is from.” Jesus cries out: “You know me, and you know where I am from. I have not come on my own. But the one who sent me is true… I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.” They know his village; they do not know his Father. “Then they tried to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.” Jesus is not a victim of chance. His hour is in the Father's hands, and when it comes he will give himself freely. On this Friday of abstinence, as we walk the Way of the Cross, we learn from him to trust our own hours to the Father: “My times are in your hand.”
outline: Ask: have you ever been disliked simply for doing what was right?
Wisdom 2 and the plot against the just.
Point 2 · His hour had not yet come
Jesus free and sovereign in his Passion.
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted.”
live: Be inconvenient for good (Wisdom 2:12)
Stand gently but firmly for what is right in one situation today, even if it costs you.
Walk the Way of the Cross
Pray the Stations today, at church or at home, and keep abstinence with love.
2027-03-12.prayer: Lord God, the righteous one was mocked and condemned, yet you were near to him and raised him up. Make us faithful when goodness is inconvenient, and teach us to place our times in your hands. Be near to all who are brokenhearted today. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The Just One who was condemned to a shameful death offered himself freely when his hour came. At the altar that hour is made present: his Body given, his Blood poured out for us.

2027-03-13.title: Saturday of the Fourth Week of Lent
readings: I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter
O Lord, my God, in you I take refuge
Does the Messiah come from Galilee?
2027-03-13.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet.
2027-03-13.verse: The police answered, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”
theo: Jeremiah, the prophet of tears, discovers that people from his own town, Anathoth, are plotting to kill him. “It was the LORD who made it known to me, and I knew.” Until then he had not suspected anything: “But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter.” They said: “Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, let us cut him off from the land of the living, so that his name will no longer be remembered!” Jeremiah does not take revenge with his own hands. He places his cause before the LORD of hosts, who judges righteously and tries the heart and the mind: “to you I have committed my cause.” His cry for retribution is honest, but the deeper movement is trust. The Church reads this passage on the threshold of Passiontide because Jeremiah is a living image of Christ, the true Lamb of God, who will be led to the slaughter and will not open his mouth, and who will commit his cause, and his spirit, into the Father's hands. The Psalm prays it with him: “O LORD my God, in you I take refuge.”

In the Gospel Jesus has spoken on the last day of the feast of Booths, and the crowd is divided. Some say: “This is really the prophet.” Others: “This is the Messiah.” Others object: the Messiah must come from Bethlehem, not Galilee. The irony is that Jesus was born in Bethlehem, but they do not know it. The Temple police, sent to arrest him, come back empty-handed. Asked why, they give one of the most beautiful testimonies in the Gospel: “Never has anyone spoken like this!” They have been disarmed by a word. The Pharisees scorn them and the crowd: “this crowd, which does not know the law… they are accursed.” Then one voice rises from among the rulers: Nicodemus, “who had gone to Jesus before,” by night. He does not yet confess Jesus openly; he only asks for fairness: “Our law does not judge people without first giving them a hearing… does it?” They mock him too. But this small courage will grow: on Good Friday Nicodemus will come to the cross carrying a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for the burial of Jesus. Lent asks us: will we let Jesus' word disarm us, and will we find courage, even a little, to speak for him?
outline: Ask: has a word ever stopped you in your tracks?
Point 2 · Never has anyone spoken like this
From a question to a hundred pounds of myrrh.
“O LORD my God, in you I take refuge.”
live: Commit your cause to God (Jeremiah 11:20)
Bring to God one injustice you have suffered, and give up the wish for revenge.
Speak one fair word
Like Nicodemus, speak up gently for someone who is being judged without a hearing.
2027-03-13.prayer: Lord God, you saw Jeremiah led like a lamb to the slaughter, and you sent your Son, the true Lamb, to take away the sin of the world. Let his word disarm our hearts, and give us the courage of Nicodemus to speak for him and for the truth. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Before Communion we hear: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. The gentle lamb of Jeremiah's lament is fulfilled in Christ, who gives himself to us on the altar.

2027-03-15.title: Monday of the Fifth Week of Lent
readings: I am to die, though I have done none of the wicked things they charge against me
If I should walk in the valley of darkness, no evil would I fear, for you are there with me
Let anyone among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her
2027-03-15.alt: Lenten weekday of the fifth week. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. From the Fifth Sunday of Lent crosses and images may be veiled until the Passion is celebrated (where the bishops' conference allows). Liturgical colour: violet. The shorter form of the first reading begins at Daniel 13:41c.
2027-03-15.verse: Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.”
theo: The last fortnight of Lent opens with two women on trial. The first is Susanna, from the Greek chapters of Daniel. She is innocent. Two elders, judges of the people, lust after her and trap her alone in her husband's garden: give in, or we will swear we caught you with a young man. Her answer is one of the bravest sentences in the Bible: “I choose not to do it; I will fall into your hands, rather than sin in the sight of the Lord.” The elders keep their threat, the assembly believes them because they are elders, and she is condemned to death. Through her tears she looks up to heaven and prays: “O eternal God, you know what is secret and are aware of all things before they come to be.” The Lord hears her. He stirs up the spirit of a young lad named Daniel, who cries out, “I want no part in shedding this woman's blood!” He separates the two witnesses and asks each a simple question: under what tree? One says a mastic tree, the other an evergreen oak, and the lie collapses. The whole assembly blesses God, “who saves those who hope in him.” The Psalm is Susanna's prayer and ours: even in the darkest valley I fear no evil, for you are with me.

The second woman is guilty. Early in the morning, in the Temple, the scribes and Pharisees set before Jesus a woman caught in adultery: Moses commanded such women to be stoned; “Now what do you say?” It is a trap for him more than a trial for her. Jesus bends down and writes with his finger on the ground. When they press him, he stands and says: “Let anyone among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” Then he writes again. One by one they go away, “beginning with the elders.” St Augustine's famous phrase sums up the scene: two were left, misery and mercy. Jesus does not pretend that sin is nothing. He says both things: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.” Put the two readings side by side and Lent becomes clear. God defends the innocent who trust him, and he lifts up the guilty who come before him. What he will not tolerate is the hard heart that stands ready with a stone. As the crosses are veiled and the Passion draws near, we are invited to drop our stones, to stop judging, and to let Jesus speak to us the word of pardon and of new life.
outline: Ask: have you ever been judged unfairly, or judged someone else too quickly?
Point 2 · The God who sees in secret
Daniel's wisdom and the collapse of the lie.
Jesus, the woman and the stones.
“Neither do I condemn you. Go your way, and from now on do not sin again.”
live: Drop your stone (John 8:7)
Name one person you have been judging harshly, and pray for them by name today.
Choose rather than sin (Daniel 13:23)
Where you are being pressed to do wrong, decide today, with Susanna, to say no.
2027-03-15.prayer: O God, you defend the innocent who hope in you and you pardon the sinner who turns to you. Give us the courage of Susanna, who chose death rather than sin, and the humility to drop the stones we hold against others. Speak to us your word of mercy, Lord Jesus, and send us on our way to sin no more. Amen.
altar: At every Mass we say: Lord, I am not worthy. No one approaches the altar without sin; we come because the one who did not condemn the woman invites us to his table and makes us new.

2027-03-16.title: Tuesday of the Fifth Week of Lent
readings: Whenever a serpent bit someone, that person would look at the serpent of bronze and live
O Lord, listen to my prayer and let my cry for help reach you
When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he
2027-03-16.alt: Lenten weekday of the fifth week. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. From the Fifth Sunday of Lent crosses and images may be veiled until the Passion is celebrated (where the bishops' conference allows). Liturgical colour: violet.
2027-03-16.verse: So Jesus said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own, but I speak these things as the Father instructed me.”
theo: The people of Israel are on the long road around Edom, and they lose patience. They complain against God and against Moses: why did you bring us out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? “There is no food and no water, and we detest this miserable food.” The miserable food is the manna, the bread from heaven. Then poisonous serpents come among them, and many die. The people confess, “We have sinned,” and Moses prays for them. God's remedy is strange: “Make a poisonous serpent, and set it on a pole; and everyone who is bitten shall look at it and live.” Moses makes a serpent of bronze, and whoever looks at it lives. The very image of what was killing them, lifted up, becomes the sign of healing. The book of Wisdom later explains that it was not the bronze that saved them but God, the Saviour of all (Wisdom 16:7), and King Hezekiah would one day break the bronze serpent because people had begun to burn incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). The sign points beyond itself. The Psalm is the cry of all who are dying in the desert: “Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you,” and its confidence that the Lord looks down from heaven “to set free those who were doomed to die.”

Jesus himself gave us the key to this reading when he said to Nicodemus: “just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). In today's Gospel he speaks of the same lifting up: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he.” In John's Gospel, to be lifted up means two things at once: to be raised on the cross and to be exalted in glory. “I am he” echoes the name God revealed to Moses at the burning bush, “I AM.” On the cross, where Jesus looks most powerless, his divine identity will be revealed. He who bears the poison of our sin is lifted up, and whoever looks to him in faith lives. Jesus also warns that those who refuse to believe “will die in your sins”; the remedy is offered, but it must be looked at. These days the crucifix in our churches may be veiled in purple. The veil teaches us to long for the moment on Good Friday when it will be uncovered and we will be invited: behold the wood of the Cross. Then we will look, and live.
outline: Ask: where do you look when you are hurting?
Complaining about the bread from heaven.
The Son of Man lifted up on the cross.
“When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he.”
live: Look and live (Numbers 21:8)
Spend five quiet minutes today simply looking at a crucifix, and tell Jesus what is poisoning your life.
Stop complaining
For one whole day, turn every complaint into a short prayer of trust.
2027-03-16.prayer: Lord Jesus, lifted up on the cross like the serpent in the desert, we look to you and live. Heal the poison of our sin, forgive our complaining, and teach us to trust the Father on the long road. Show us that you are he, the Son who always does what pleases the Father. Amen.
altar: At Mass the priest lifts up the Host and the chalice: behold the Lamb of God. We look at the one who was lifted up on the cross, and we receive the medicine of eternal life.

2027-03-17.title: Wednesday of the Fifth Week of Lent
readings: He has sent his angel and delivered his servants who trusted in him
To you glory and praise for evermore
If the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed
2027-03-17.alt: Lenten weekday of the fifth week. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. From the Fifth Sunday of Lent crosses and images may be veiled until the Passion is celebrated (where the bishops' conference allows). Liturgical colour: violet. Commemoration of St Patrick, bishop (its collect may be used). In Ireland, and in some other places, St Patrick is kept as a solemnity or feast.
2027-03-17.verse: Then Jesus said to the Jews who had believed in him, “If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”
theo: King Nebuchadnezzar has set up a golden statue, and everyone must fall down before it when the music plays. Three young Jews, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, refuse. Brought before the furious king, they give an answer that has strengthened believers ever since: “If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire and out of your hand, O king, let him deliver us. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods.” But if not: their faithfulness does not depend on being rescued. The furnace is heated seven times hotter and they are thrown in bound. Then the king leaps up in amazement: “I see four men unbound, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are not hurt; and the fourth has the appearance of a god.” The Fathers saw in the fourth figure a foreshadowing of the Son of God, who comes into our fire. Instead of the usual Psalm, the Church today sings part of the hymn of the three young men from the Greek text of Daniel: “Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our ancestors, and to be praised and highly exalted forever.”

In the Gospel Jesus speaks of another kind of freedom: “If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” His hearers protest that as children of Abraham they have never been slaves. Jesus answers: “everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin… So if the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” The debate in this chapter is sharp, and it reflects the painful arguments between the early Christians and the synagogue of John's day; it is never a licence for contempt of the Jewish people, from whom, as Jesus says elsewhere, salvation comes (John 4:22). Today the Church remembers St Patrick (about 385 to about 461). Captured as a boy in Britain and enslaved in Ireland, he learned to pray on the hillsides while tending sheep. He escaped, became a priest and a bishop, and went back freely to the land of his slavery to bring it the Gospel. In his Confession he writes (in substance) that he was like a stone lying deep in the mud until the Mighty One lifted him up. Patrick knew both kinds of slavery and both kinds of freedom. Like the three young men, he served God whether or not he was spared, and the truth made him free.
outline: Ask: what would you refuse to do, even if it cost you everything?
Point 2 · The fourth man in the fire
God walks with us in the furnace.
Point 3 · The truth will make you free
Slavery to sin, freedom in the Son; St Patrick.
“If the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.”
live: Refuse the golden statue (Daniel 3:18)
Name one idol in your life, money, approval, a habit, and refuse to bow to it today.
Continue in his word (John 8:31)
Read and pray over one chapter of the Gospel of Mark today, preparing for Palm Sunday.
2027-03-17.prayer: Lord God of our ancestors, blessed are you and highly exalted for ever. Give us the faith of the three young men, who served you whether or not they were rescued, and walk with us in every fire. Lord Jesus, make us free from the slavery of sin. Through the prayers of St Patrick, who returned in love to the land of his captivity, make us bold witnesses of the Gospel. Amen.
altar: The Son who makes us free gives himself at the altar. In the Eucharist he walks with us in the fire of daily life, as the fourth figure walked with the three young men.

2027-03-18.title: Thursday of the Fifth Week of Lent
readings: You shall be the ancestor of a multitude of nations
The Lord remembers his covenant for ever
Your ancestor Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day
2027-03-18.alt: Lenten weekday of the fifth week. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. From the Fifth Sunday of Lent crosses and images may be veiled until the Passion is celebrated (where the bishops' conference allows). Liturgical colour: violet. Commemoration of St Cyril of Jerusalem, bishop and Doctor of the Church (its collect may be used).
2027-03-18.verse: Jesus said to them, “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.”
theo: Abram is ninety-nine years old and childless when God appears to him again. He falls on his face, and God speaks: “As for me, this is my covenant with you: You shall be the ancestor of a multitude of nations. No longer shall your name be Abram, but your name shall be Abraham.” A new name means a new mission. God binds himself with an everlasting covenant, “to be God to you and to your offspring after you,” and asks Abraham to keep it, he and his descendants. The whole history of Israel hangs on this promise, and so does ours: St Paul will say that all who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to the promise (Galatians 3:29). The Psalm answers with wonder that God never forgets: “He is mindful of his covenant forever, of the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations.” In the last days of Lent, as the elect prepare for Baptism, the Church reminds us that God's covenant is older and stronger than our failures.

In the Gospel the argument about Abraham reaches its peak. Jesus says: “whoever keeps my word will never see death.” His hearers object that Abraham died, and the prophets died: “Who do you claim to be?” Jesus answers that Abraham “rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.” They reply, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” Then comes the most daring sentence in the Gospel: “Very truly, I tell you, before Abraham was, I am.” He does not say I was, but I AM, the name of God revealed to Moses. Some take up stones, judging it blasphemy, and Jesus slips away from the Temple. When John writes “the Jews” in such scenes, he usually means the leaders and opponents in Jerusalem, not the whole Jewish people, of whom Jesus, Mary and the apostles were members; the Church firmly rejects any use of these texts to blame the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4). Today we remember St Cyril of Jerusalem (about 313 to 386), bishop of the city where these words were spoken. Around the year 350 he gave his famous Catechetical Lectures to those preparing for Easter Baptism, near the place of the Cross and the empty tomb, and after Easter he explained to the newly baptized the mysteries they had received. Exiled three times in the struggles against the Arian heresy, he held fast to the faith that Jesus is truly God, the I AM before Abraham.
outline: Ask: what does your name mean, and who gave it to you?
A new name and an everlasting covenant.
The promise looks forward to Christ.
Point 3 · Before Abraham was, I am
Jesus, the eternal Son; St Cyril, teacher of the faith.
live: Remember the covenant (Psalm 105:8)
Thank God today for your Baptism, the day you entered his covenant; find out its date if you do not know it.
Keep his word (John 8:51)
Choose one word of Jesus from this week's Gospels and live it today.
2027-03-18.prayer: God of Abraham, you never forget your covenant. Thank you for making us, in Christ, heirs of your promise. Lord Jesus, before Abraham was, you are; we adore you as true God and true man. Through the prayers of St Cyril of Jerusalem, who taught the faith to the newly baptized, keep us faithful to our Baptism and lead the elect safely to Easter. Amen.
altar: St Cyril taught the newly baptized (in substance): do not regard the bread and wine as plain bread and wine, for they are the Body and Blood of Christ as the Lord declared; let faith assure you. At every Mass the eternal I AM gives himself to us.

2027-03-19.title: St Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
readings: The Lord God will give him the throne of his ancestor David
His dynasty shall last for ever
Joseph did as the angel of the Lord commanded him
2027-03-19.alt: Solemnity. The readings of Friday of the Fifth Week of Lent give way to those of the solemnity. The Gloria and the Creed are said; the Gospel acclamation is sung without Alleluia, as throughout Lent. Because today is a solemnity, the Friday obligation of abstinence does not bind this year (Code of Canon Law, can. 1251); many still choose another act of penance or charity. When 19 March falls in Holy Week the solemnity is moved, but in 2027 it is kept on its own day. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-03-19.verse: When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him; he took her as his wife
theo: In the middle of the last fortnight of Lent the Church puts on white for the man to whom God entrusted his greatest treasures. St Joseph never speaks a single word in the Gospels, yet everything depends on his listening. The first reading takes us back a thousand years before him. King David wants to build a house for God, and God answers through the prophet Nathan that he will build a house for David instead: “I will raise up your offspring after you… and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me… Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me.” By the time of Jesus the royal line of David had fallen into obscurity; its heir was a carpenter in Nazareth. Matthew's genealogy ends with “Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.” Notice the care: Joseph is not called the father who begot Jesus, but the husband of Mary. Yet through Joseph's legal fatherhood, through his giving the child a name, Jesus is grafted into the house of David. The angel greets him as “Joseph, son of David.” God's promise to David passes through the hands of this silent, faithful man.

Matthew tells us what Joseph faced. Mary, already betrothed to him, “was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.” Joseph, “being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.” His righteousness is not cold law; it is mercy and reverence before a mystery he does not yet understand. Then the angel speaks in a dream: “do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” And Joseph's whole answer is action: “When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him; he took her as his wife.” St Paul's words about Abraham in the second reading fit Joseph perfectly: “Hoping against hope, he believed,” and his faith “was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Where the alternative Gospel is read, Luke shows Joseph and Mary searching three days for the twelve-year-old Jesus and finding him in the Temple. Mary says, “your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety,” and Jesus answers, “Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” Joseph accepts that the boy he raises belongs first to another Father, and still Jesus “went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them.” The Son of God learned to work, to pray the psalms and to keep the law at Joseph's side.

The Church has slowly come to see how great this hidden man is. Blessed Pius IX declared St Joseph Patron of the Universal Church in 1870; Leo XIII wrote about him in Quamquam Pluries (1889); St John Paul II called him the Guardian of the Redeemer (Redemptoris Custos, 1989); and Pope Francis, in Patris Corde (2020), described him as a beloved, tender, obedient, accepting, creatively courageous and working father, a father in the shadow. Joseph is patron of families, of workers, of fathers, of those who must make hard decisions in the night, and of a happy death, since he died, as tradition holds, in the arms of Jesus and Mary. In many parishes in Kerala this day brings a festive meal for the poor and for all who come, remembering the man who fed the Holy Family with the work of his hands. Even in Lent, today is a day of joy. We ask St Joseph to guard the Church as he guarded the child and his mother, and to teach us his way: to listen, to rise, and to do what God asks without many words.
conn: Son of David.
Joseph's genealogy in Matthew runs from Abraham through David. By naming the child, Joseph gives Jesus his legal place in David's line (Matthew 1:20–21; Luke 1:27).
Betrothal.

In Jewish custom betrothal was already a binding marriage; the bride lived in her father's house until the husband took her to his home. That is why Matthew calls Joseph her husband before they lived together.
Four dreams.
In Matthew, God speaks to Joseph four times in dreams: to take Mary (1:20), to flee to Egypt (2:13), to return (2:19–20) and to settle in Galilee (2:22). Each time he obeys at once.
Righteous.
The Greek word dikaios describes one who lives faithfully by God's law. Joseph's righteousness shows itself in mercy and in obedience to God's new word.
The craftsman.
Matthew 13:55 calls Jesus the carpenter's son; the Greek tekton means a builder or craftsman in wood and stone. Joseph is honoured on 1 May as St Joseph the Worker.
A feast in Lent.
As a solemnity, today has the Gloria and the Creed, and the Friday abstinence does not bind (can. 1251). In some years 19 March falls in Holy Week and the solemnity is moved.
altar: Joseph held in his arms the Body of the Lord that we receive at the altar. St Bernard compares him to the patriarch Joseph, who stored bread for a starving world: this Joseph guarded the living Bread come down from heaven.

St Joseph is named in the Eucharistic Prayers, after the Virgin Mary, since Pope Francis added his name in 2013 to the Second, Third and Fourth Eucharistic Prayers. The silent guardian stands beside us at every Mass.
outline: Ask: who are the quiet people who have protected and provided for you without many words?
God's promise passes through a carpenter.
Mercy, reverence and a dilemma in the night.
The faith of Abraham in the heart of Joseph.
He went down with them and was obedient to them.
A carpenter's hands holding a sleeping child.
“He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.”
live: Do what God asks (Matthew 1:24)
Name one thing God has been asking of you, and do it today without delay.
Protect someone
Like Joseph, take care of someone vulnerable in your family or neighbourhood this week.
Work as prayer
Offer your work today to God through St Joseph, and do it well and honestly.
Pray for a good death
Pray for the dying today, and ask St Joseph, patron of a happy death, to be with them.
fathers: St Bernard of Clairvaux (in substance)

The patriarch Joseph stored up grain, not for himself but for all the people; this Joseph received the living Bread from heaven and kept it for himself and for the whole world. He is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord set over his household.
St Bernardine of Siena (in substance)

Whenever God chooses someone for a special grace or a high office, he gives that person all the gifts needed for it. So it was with Joseph, chosen by the eternal Father as the faithful foster-father and guardian of his chief treasures, his Son and his Son's mother.
St Teresa of Avila (in substance)

I took the glorious St Joseph as my advocate and patron, and I do not remember ever asking anything of him that he failed to grant. I would like to persuade everyone to be devoted to this glorious saint.
magis: Catechism 437, 497
The angel's message to Joseph; the virginal conception of Jesus by the Holy Spirit.
Catechism 532–534
The hidden life at Nazareth and the finding in the Temple.
Catechism 1014
St Joseph, patron of a happy death.
Redemptoris Custos (St John Paul II, 1989)
Joseph, Guardian of the Redeemer, in the life of Christ and of the Church.
Patris Corde (Pope Francis, 2020)
Joseph, a beloved, tender, obedient, accepting, creatively courageous and working father, a father in the shadow.
saints: St Joseph

Of the house of David, a craftsman of Nazareth, husband of the Virgin Mary and legal father of Jesus. He protected Mary and the child, fled with them to Egypt, raised Jesus at Nazareth and, according to tradition, died before Jesus' public ministry. Patron of the Universal Church (1870).
This week
15–20 Mar: Lenten weekdays of the fifth week; 17 Mar: St Patrick; 18 Mar: St Cyril of Jerusalem (commemorations). 21 Mar: Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord; Holy Week begins.
2027-03-19.prayer: Grant, we pray, almighty God, that by Saint Joseph's intercession your Church may constantly watch over the unfolding of the mysteries of human salvation, whose beginnings you entrusted to his faithful care. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: St Joseph, son of David, husband of Mary and guardian of the Redeemer, protect our families, our workers and our Church. Teach us to listen to God in the night, to rise and obey, and to love Jesus and Mary as you loved them. Be with us and with all the dying at the hour of our death. Amen.

2027-03-20.title: Saturday of the Fifth Week of Lent
readings: I will make them one nation in the land
The Lord will guard us as a shepherd guards his flock
Jesus was about to die to gather into one the dispersed children of God
2027-03-20.alt: Lenten weekday of the fifth week. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. From the Fifth Sunday of Lent crosses and images may be veiled until the Passion is celebrated (where the bishops' conference allows). Liturgical colour: violet. Tomorrow Holy Week begins with Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord; parishes may announce the time and place of the blessing of palms and the procession.
2027-03-20.verse: He did not say this on his own, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.
theo: On the eve of Holy Week the Church reads a promise of unity. Ezekiel had seen the kingdom of David split into two, Israel and Judah, and then both scattered in exile. Now God promises: “I will take the people of Israel from the nations… I will make them one nation in the land… and one king shall be king over them all. Never again shall they be two nations.” He will cleanse them from their idols, give them “one shepherd,” his servant David, and make “a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant… My dwelling place shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” Instead of a Psalm, we sing Jeremiah's song of the shepherd who gathers: “He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will keep him as a shepherd a flock… I will turn their mourning into joy.”

The Gospel shows how this gathering will happen. Jesus has just raised Lazarus at Bethany. Many believe in him; others report to the authorities. The council meets in fear: if we let him go on, “the Romans will come and destroy both our holy place and our nation.” Caiaphas, the high priest that year, gives a cold political calculation: “it is better for you to have one man die for the people than to have the whole nation destroyed.” John sees a hidden prophecy in it: Jesus was indeed about to die for the nation, “and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God.” What Caiaphas meant as expediency, God turned into salvation. We must read this carefully: the decision belongs to a small group of leaders in a frightened hour, and the Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597). In truth, Christ died for the sins of all of us. The chapter ends with pilgrims in the Temple asking each other, “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival, will he?” Tomorrow we have the answer: he comes, riding on a colt, to lay down his life and gather us into one.
outline: Ask: what divides your family, parish or village, and who can bring it back together?
Point 2 · One man for the people
Caiaphas speaks more than he knows.
Point 3 · Will he come to the festival?
On the threshold of Holy Week.
“To gather into one the dispersed children of God.”
live: Gather, do not scatter (John 11:52)
Take one step today to heal a division in your family or among friends: a call, a visit, a word of peace.
Prepare for Holy Week
Plan your week now: the Palm Sunday procession, confession, the Chrism Mass if possible, and the Triduum.
2027-03-20.prayer: Good Shepherd, you laid down your life to gather into one the scattered children of God. Heal the divisions in our families, our parishes and among Christians. As Holy Week begins, let us go up with you to Jerusalem, to your cross and to your resurrection. Amen.
altar: The Eucharist is the sacrament of unity: one bread, one body. Around the altar Christ gathers into one the dispersed children of God, as he promised by his death.

2027-03-22.title: Monday of Holy Week
readings: Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights (First Song of the Servant)
The Lord is my light and my salvation
Leave her alone. She bought it so that she might keep it for the day of my burial
2027-03-22.alt: Holy Week. Lent continues until the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Thursday. No Gloria, no Alleluia. Liturgical colour: violet. In some dioceses the Chrism Mass is celebrated on one of the first days of Holy Week, so that priests from distant parishes can come; ask in your parish.
2027-03-22.verse: Mary took a pound of costly perfume made of pure nard, anointed Jesus' feet, and wiped them with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.
theo: Holy Week has begun. Yesterday we walked with palms; this week the Church walks with Jesus, day by day, towards the Upper Room, the cross and the empty tomb. On the first three days the readings are quiet and searching. The first readings give us the Songs of the Servant of the Lord from the Book of Isaiah, four poems about a mysterious servant who is gentle, faithful, rejected and finally glorified through suffering. The Gospels take us into the last days of Jesus in Bethany and Jerusalem. Today the first Song begins: “Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my spirit upon him.” This servant does not shout or push his way through the streets. “A bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench.” He is given “as a covenant to the people, a light to the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon.” At the Jordan the Father had said of Jesus, “with you I am well pleased”; St Matthew quotes this very song to describe him (Matthew 12:18–21). The Psalm is the prayer of the Servant as the darkness gathers: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

The Gospel is set “six days before the Passover” in Bethany, at the home of Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. A dinner is given for him. Martha serves, as she always does; Lazarus sits at table, living proof of the power of Jesus; and Mary does something that fills the whole house. She takes “a pound of costly perfume made of pure nard,” anoints the feet of Jesus and wipes them with her hair. A pound of nard was a fortune, about a year's wages for a labourer. Judas protests in the name of the poor, but St John tells us plainly that he did not care about the poor: he kept the common purse and stole from it. Jesus defends Mary: “Leave her alone. She bought it so that she might keep it for the day of my burial.” Mary understands what the others have not yet grasped: the one she loves is going to die, and love cannot measure its gifts. Her anointing points to the burial of Jesus on Friday, and beyond it to the morning when other women will come with spices and find the tomb empty.

The scene ends with a shadow. Many people come to see Jesus and Lazarus, and many believe; so “the chief priests planned to put Lazarus to death as well.” St John speaks of a small circle of leaders who feared for their authority and for the nation under Rome (John 11:47–50). The Church teaches clearly that the Passion cannot be blamed on the Jewish people as a whole, then or now (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597–598); every sinner, and so each of us, had a part in the sufferings of Christ. On this Monday the question for us is simple: are we Martha, serving; Lazarus, simply being with him; Mary, pouring out what is precious; or Judas, calculating? Holy Week invites us to break our alabaster jar for him: our time, our pride, our tears, our love. And Jesus, the gentle Servant, will not break the bruised reed of our weakness.
conn: The Servant Songs.

Four poems in Isaiah 42:1–7, 49:1–6, 50:4–9 and 52:13–53:12. The Church reads them on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week and on Good Friday. The Servant is Israel called to be a light, and in the fullest sense Jesus himself (Acts 8:32–35).
Six days before the Passover.
John counts down to the Passover as to the hour of Jesus. The anointing at Bethany opens the final week.
Pure nard.
An oil from a plant of the Himalayas, carried by traders to the Mediterranean. Three hundred denarii was close to a year's wage; a denarius was a day's pay (Matthew 20:2).
Anointed for burial.
The bodies of the dead were anointed with spices (John 19:39–40). Christ means the Anointed One; Mary anoints the King for his throne, the cross.
Holy Week in the parish.

Monday to Wednesday are weekdays of Lent with their own readings. Many parishes hold a penitential service and extra confessions; some keep Tenebrae, the ancient service of darkness, on Wednesday evening.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Do you wish to be a faithful soul? Anoint the feet of Jesus with Mary by living well; wipe them with your hair: if you have more than you need, give it to the poor, and you have wiped the feet of the Lord. The house was filled with the fragrance: the whole world is filled with the good report of what she did.
St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)
The Lord received ointment on his head so that he might breathe incorruption upon the Church.
outline: Ask: what is the most precious thing you have ever given away?
He does not break the bruised reed.
The Psalm of trust as the Passion begins.
“The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.”
live: Break your alabaster jar (John 12:3)
Give Jesus something costly this week: an hour of prayer, a quarrel ended, a confession long delayed.
Do not break the bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3)
Be gentle with one person who is weak, discouraged or failing.
Plan Holy Week
Write down the times of the Holy Thursday, Good Friday and Easter Vigil services and plan your family's week around them.
2027-03-22.prayer: Lord Jesus, gentle Servant of the Father, you did not break the bruised reed or quench the dimly burning wick. As Mary poured out her perfume at your feet, let us pour out our love for you this Holy Week. Free us from the calculating heart, be our light and our salvation, and bring us with you through the cross to the joy of Easter. Amen.
altar: Mary anointed the body of Jesus for his burial. At the altar we receive that same Body, given up and risen, and the fragrance of his sacrifice fills the whole Church.

2027-03-23.title: Tuesday of Holy Week
readings: I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Second Song of the Servant)
I will sing of your salvation
One of you will betray me. Before the cock crows, you will have denied me three times
2027-03-23.alt: Holy Week. Lent continues until the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Thursday. No Gloria, no Alleluia. Liturgical colour: violet. The memorial of St Turibius of Mogrovejo, bishop, is not celebrated this year, because no memorial is kept during Holy Week.
2027-03-23.verse: I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.
theo: Today the second Song of the Servant lets the Servant himself speak. “The LORD called me before I was born, while I was in my mother's womb he named me.” God has shaped him like a sharp sword and a polished arrow, hidden in his quiver until the right moment.
